items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-12 Senior Bankruptcy Specialist with the Agency’s Small Business/Self- Employed Division, Specialty Collection– Insolvency Office in Houston, Texas. On September 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her and subjected her to a hostile work environment on the bases of disability (Major Depression, Recurrence, Somatic Symptoms Disorder, Generalized Anxiety, TIA, Myofascial Pain, Acute Stress Disorder) and reprisal (prior protected EEO activity) when: 1. 1.Beginning February 2021 to the present, she has been denied paid leave under the Family Medical and Leave Act (FMLA); 2. On June 19, 2021, a manager reassigned all of a retired co-worker’s complex cases to her; 3. On August 3, 2021, she was denied eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave; 4. On August 24, 2021, her final appeal of a requested reasonable accommodation was denied; and 5. On October 26, 2021, her supervisor denied her official time request to work on her EEO complaint. Claims 1 & 3 – Leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) Complainant challenged leave issues, including her receipt of Absent Without Leave (AWOL) charges and placement in Leave Without Pay (LWOP) status in a prior EEO complaint before an EEOC Administrative Judge. On May 25, 2022, the Administrative Judge in that case found that the Agency had proven that it had placed Complainant in AWOL and LWOP status on various dates in February and March 2021, because Complainant had depleted her available paid leave balances and failed to report to work. In the instant complaint, Complainant again raised leave issues previously adjudicated, including her February and March 2021 receipt of AWOL charges and placement in LWOP status. Complainant also alleges that on August 3, 2021, her manager denied eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave. Complainant’s first-line supervisor (Supervisor1) explained that management’s calculations showed that Complainant had exhausted her paid, available sick leave by March 2021. Specifically, the Agency’s February 26, 2021, letter to Complainant regarding her request for FMLA provided that Complainant had only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA to use between March 1, 2021, and December 3, 2021. As such, on March 1, 2021, and on other dates, Supervisor notified Complainant that she had no paid leave available to use under FMLA. On various dates, including August 3, 2021, Supervisor granted Complainant FMLA-LWOP, rather than paid leave. Complainant did not request an audit of her leave until August 5, 2021. The audit of Complainant’s leave, conducted by a payroll representative, showed that Complainant had some paid leave available to use under FMLA. Accordingly, management retroactively granted Complainant paid leave, including for August 3, 2021. Complainant conceded that she ultimately received all paid leave that she requested and was entitled to receive. Complainant did not identify any similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding leave. Claim 2 – Reassignment of Casework In June 2021, one of Complainant’s GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers retired. Complainant claimed that Supervisor emailed Complainant (a GS- 12) and two other GS-12 employees in the group to inform them that the now- retired employee’s cases would be reassigned among the three GS-12s. Complainant asserted that she should not have been reassigned this casework because she had previously submitted a request for reasonable accommodation and believed she should have been on indefinite weather and safety leave. 2 The Administrative Judge found that Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave, and that the Agency had met all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. The appeal is currently pending and docketed as EEOC [number removed]. Supervisor explained that she reassigned the cases because it was her job to assign inventory to employees in her group. Supervisor also explained that all reassigned work was appropriate for Complainant’s grade level. Supervisor further explained that the work was split among Complainant and the two other GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists in the group, based upon the alphabetical order of case names. The documentary record also contains a spreadsheet, provided by Supervisor1, showing the case assignments to Complainant and the two other Bankruptcy Specialists in the group. The record is devoid of similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding this claim. Claim 4 –Reasonable Accommodations On May 6, 2021, Complainant requested the following accommodations: (1) that her manager and/or secretary assistant print and mail her letters; and (2) a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her reasonable accommodation request to include reassignment. Complainant concedes that her medical impairment does not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. The Agency’s Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator met with Complainant on May 21, 2021, to hold an interactive meeting. Regarding her request for reduced workload and/or reassignment, the Agency issued a denial, noting that there was no medical explanation supporting Complainant’s need for such accommodations. The Agency’s denial also noted that lowering Complainant’s caseload would lower performance or production standards and would compromise the Agency’s ability to achieve its mission. Moreover, with an inventory of then only 25 cases, the undisputed record showed that Complainant already maintained a caseload well below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below the number of cases she typically held. 3 Regarding her request for reassignment, the Agency’s denial noted that Complainant was not eligible for reassignment because it is the accommodation of last resort (i.e., granted only when an employee is unable to meet the essential functions of her position). For example, to support a previous 2018 request for reduced inventory, Complainant’s psychologist had noted that Complainant desired a reduced inventory of approximately 38-40 cases. When Complainant requested reassignment as a reasonable accommodation in March 2020, the Agency explained that Complainant failed to submit medical documentation supporting that she was unable to meet the essential functions of her position. Rather, the evidence showed that Complainant wished to be reassigned because she had an unpleasant working relationship with her supervisors, and not because of any medical impairment’s effect on her ability to perform the essential functions of her job. To accommodate Complainant’s physical limitations, in response to Complainant’s May 6, 2021 reasonable accommodation request, the Agency approved Complainant to receive a small portable printer so that she could print and mail letters to taxpayers. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. Before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket cancelling the printer because she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Complainant later averred that she would not be able to lift either the smaller printer or its paper. The Agency denied Complainant’s request for reconsideration of her reasonable accommodation denial. On July 12, 2021, Complainant appealed the Agency’s denial of her reconsideration request. On August 24, 2021, the Director of Collection Operations (Director) denied Complainant’s appeal. The denial noted that Complainant had summarily rejected the Agency’s offer to provide her with a smaller portable printer that she could lift. Further, the denial noted that Complainant had an already-reduced workload and was not eligible for reassignment because she was capable of performing the essential functions of her job. Claim 5 – Official Time On October 20, 2021, Complainant requested to use official time from approximately 10:30 a.m. on October 20 through 11:30 a.m. on October 21, 2021, to respond to an EEO Investigator’s request that Complainant complete an affidavit for the instant complaint. Complainant availed herself of six hours of official time on October 20, 2021, and four hours on October 21, 2021. Despite being provided these hours, Complainant did not complete her affidavit and requested additional time on October 25, 2021. On October 25, 2021, Supervisor approved Complainant’s request to use additional official time that day. On October 26, 2021, Complainant emailed the Department of Treasury, Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request an extension of her deadline to complete her affidavit. In response, OCRD noted that Complainant could request an extension from the investigator if she needed more time to complete the affidavit. After receiving OCRD’s response, Complainant asked Supervisor for official time to complete the affidavit that day. When Supervisor asked Complainant if she had completed the affidavit, Complainant told Supervisor that she had two questions remaining. Because Complainant had already received approximately 18 hours of official time and because OCRD had instructed Complainant to contact the investigator if she needed an extension of her deadline, Supervisor denied Complainant’s request to continue working on her affidavit on official time on October 26, 2021. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ. Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency. In the decision, the AJ determined that the alleged incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive to establish a hostile work environment. Further, the AJ found that there was no evidence demonstrating that the conduct at issue was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus. For example, Complainant failed to show that similarly situated employees outside of her protected classes were treated more favorably by being granted FMLA or other leave entitlements. Additionally, the record evidence showed that the reassigned cases from the retired, former coworker were split equally amongst Complainant and two of her Bankruptcy Specialists coworkers for unrebutted reasons relative to grade, skill level and appropriateness given Complainant’s low workload. With respect to her denial of reasonable accommodation claim, the AJ determined that in her May 6, 2021 request, Complainant requested that her manager and/or secretary assist her to print and mail her letters and also requested a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her request to include reassignment. During the investigation of the instant complaint, Complainant admitted that her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. Moreover, she did not adduce any probative evidence that previously offered accommodations—a post of duty (with telework) away from her manager and communication primarily by email—did not enable the Complainant to perform the essential functions of her position. Further, the AJ found that the record supported the Agency’s denial of Complainant’s request for a reduced inventory. An agency is not required to change production standards, e.g., to lower an employee’s quota for cases. Complainant provided no evidence that she could not adequately perform her assignments given she had an unusually low inventory of only 25 cases. Finally, the AJ concluded that the undisputed record showed, after an interactive meeting, the Agency approved Complainant for a lightweight, portable printer. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. However, before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket requesting cancellation of the printer delivery, stating that she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Management continued to print and mail her letters. As a result, the AJ found that the Agency did not deny Complainant reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. Finally, the AJ found that the Agency’s grant of 18 hours of official time was objectively reasonable for Complainant to complete her affidavit despite the investigators’ numerous questions. The record showed that Complainant’s time was spent including information and documentation she previously provided in previous complaints. The Agency was entitled to limit the Complainant’s use of official time to 18 hours to complete her affidavit for this complaint and to have her seek additional time from the investigator. Accordingly, the AJ concluded that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

# FINDINGS

## Overview
This investigation examined five distinct claims of discrimination and reprisal filed by Complainant, a GS-12 Senior Bankruptcy Specialist, based on disability and prior protected EEO activity. The investigation included a detailed review of documentary evidence, witness statements, and prior administrative determinations. An EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency, which was subsequently adopted by final order.

## Claims 1 & 3 – Denial of FMLA Leave

**Leave Depletion and AWOL/LWOP Status (February-March 2021)**

Complainant's claims regarding FMLA leave denials in February and March 2021 were previously adjudicated by an EEOC Administrative Judge on May 25, 2022. That Judge determined that the Agency properly placed Complainant in Absent Without Leave (AWOL) and Leave Without Pay (LWOP) status because Complainant had depleted her available paid leave balances and failed to report to work. Complainant's re-litigation of these same issues in the instant complaint does not present new evidence or circumstances warranting reconsideration.

**August 3, 2021 Denial of Eight Hours of Paid FMLA Sick Leave**

Supervisor1 maintained records indicating that Complainant had exhausted her paid, available sick leave by March 2021. A February 26, 2021 Agency letter informed Complainant that she possessed only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA leave available between March 1, 2021, and December 3, 2021. Consequently, on March 1, 2021, and subsequent dates, Supervisor1 notified Complainant that no paid leave remained available.

However, when Complainant requested an audit of her leave on August 5, 2021, a payroll representative's audit revealed that Complainant retained some paid leave available under FMLA. The Agency retroactively granted Complainant paid leave for August 3, 2021, and other dates as warranted. Complainant conceded that she ultimately received all paid leave to which she was entitled.

Complainant did not identify any similarly situated employees who received more favorable treatment regarding leave entitlements.

## Claim 2 – Reassignment of Casework (June 2021)

When a GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialist retired in June 2021, Supervisor1 reassigned the retired employee's cases among three GS-12 level employees, including Complainant. Complainant objected to the reassignment, asserting she should have been on indefinite weather and safety leave and therefore should not have received additional work.

The record establishes that:

- Supervisor1's reassignment decision fell within her authority to assign inventory to employees in her group
- All reassigned work was appropriate for Complainant's grade level (GS-12)
- Cases were distributed among the three GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists based on alphabetical order of case names
- Documentary evidence, including a spreadsheet provided by Supervisor1, corroborates the equitable distribution of cases

An Administrative Judge in a separate proceeding determined that Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave and that the Agency met all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. That appeal remains pending.

No evidence in the record demonstrates that similarly situated employees received more favorable treatment.

## Claim 4 – Reasonable Accommodations

**Initial Request and Interactive Meeting**

On May 6, 2021, Complainant requested: (1) assistance from her manager and/or secretary to print and mail letters; and (2) a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her request to include reassignment. The Agency's Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator conducted an interactive meeting on May 21, 2021.

**Complainant's Medical Limitations**

Critically, Complainant conceded that her medical impairment does not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. This admission substantially undermines the factual foundation for requesting reduced workload or reassignment accommodations.

**Agency Denial of Reduced Workload and Reassignment**

The Agency denied both requests based on the following:

- No medical documentation supported the need for reduced workload
- Lowering Complainant's caseload would compromise performance standards and Agency mission accomplishment
- At the time of the request, Complainant maintained only 25 cases—substantially below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below her typical historical caseload
- Reassignment constitutes an accommodation of last resort, available only when an employee cannot meet essential job functions
- Complainant failed to demonstrate inability to perform essential functions

The record reflected that Complainant's 2018 request for reduced inventory stated she desired approximately 38-40 cases, yet her contemporaneous caseload of 25 cases already fell below this threshold.

**Approval of Printer Accommodation**

The Agency approved Complainant's request for assistance printing and mailing correspondence. To address her physical limitations, management approved a small, portable printer that Complainant could operate. While awaiting delivery, management agreed to print and mail Complainant's correspondence.

However, before the printer's delivery, Complainant cancelled the order, stating she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Complainant later asserted she would be unable to lift either the portable printer or its paper—a position inconsistent with her earlier request for the device. Management continued to print and mail Complainant's letters notwithstanding the cancellation.

**Reconsideration and Appeal**

On July 12, 2021, Complainant appealed the denial of her reconsideration request. The Director of Collection Operations denied the appeal on August 24, 2021, reiterating that Complainant had rejected the Agency's offer of a lightweight portable printer and noting that she already maintained a reduced workload and was capable of performing essential job functions.

## Claim 5 – Denial of Official Time (October 26, 2021)

On October 20, 2021, Complainant requested official time to complete an affidavit in response to an EEO Investigator's request. The Agency granted Complainant:

- Six hours of official time on October 20, 2021
- Four hours of official time on October 21, 2021
- Additional official time approved on October 25, 2021

Despite receiving approximately 18 hours of official time, Complainant did not complete her affidavit. On October 26, 2021, Complainant requested additional official time, stating she had two questions remaining on the affidavit.

Supervisor1 denied this request based on: (1) the substantial official time already provided (approximately 18 hours); and (2) OCRD's instruction that Complainant contact the investigator directly to request an extension of her deadline if additional time was needed. The record indicates that Complainant's previous official time was partially devoted to information and documentation she had previously submitted in earlier complaints.

## Administrative Judge Determination

The EEOC Administrative Judge issued a summary judgment decision finding:

1. **No Hostile Work Environment**: The alleged incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute a hostile work environment. Complainant failed to establish that conduct was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus.

2. **No Comparative Evidence of Discrimination**: Complainant did not identify similarly situated employees outside her protected classes who received more favorable treatment regarding FMLA leave, case reassignments, or other employment decisions.

3. **Leave Claims**: The Agency properly maintained records of Complainant's leave balances. Upon Complainant's belated request for an audit, any discrepancies were corrected and Complainant received all paid leave to which she was entitled.

4. **Case Reassignment**: The reassignment of cases from the retired employee was appropriate, based on grade level, skill level, and Complainant's unusually low existing workload. Cases were distributed equitably among three similarly situated GS-12 employees.

5. **Reasonable Accommodations**: The Agency met its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act by:
   - Conducting an interactive meeting
   - Offering a lightweight portable printer accommodation
   - Arranging for management to print and mail correspondence during the interim period
   - Maintaining a caseload already below typical levels for Complainant's position

   Complainant's admission that her impairment did not limit essential job functions, combined with her rejection of offered accommodations, negated any violation.

6. **Official Time**: Eighteen hours of official time was objectively reasonable for completing an affidavit. The Agency's direction that Complainant request additional time directly from the investigator, consistent with OCRD guidance, was appropriate.

## Conclusion

The record supports the Administrative Judge's determination that Complainant failed to establish discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment based on disability or prior protected EEO activity. The Agency's personnel decisions were supported by legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons documented in the record.

- Supervisor1's reassignment decision fell within her authority to assign inventory to employees in her group
- All reassigned work was appropriate for Complainant's grade level (GS-12)
- Cases were distributed among the three GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists based on alphabetical order of case names
- Documentary evidence, including a spreadsheet provided by Supervisor1, corroborates the equitable distribution of cases

An Administrative Judge in a separate proceeding determined that Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave and that the Agency met all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. That appeal remains pending.

No evidence in the record demonstrates that similarly situated employees received more favorable treatment.

## Claim 4 – Reasonable Accommodations

**Initial Request and Interactive Meeting**

On May 6, 2021, Complainant requested: (1) assistance from her manager and/or secretary to print and mail letters; and (2) a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her request to include reassignment. The Agency's Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator conducted an interactive meeting on May 21, 2021.

**Complainant's Medical Limitations**

Critically, Complainant conceded that her medical impairment does not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. This admission substantially undermines the factual foundation for requesting reduced workload or reassignment accommodations.

**Agency Denial of Reduced Workload and Reassignment**

The Agency denied both requests based on the following:

- No medical documentation supported the need for reduced workload
- Lowering Complainant's caseload would compromise performance standards and Agency mission accomplishment
- At the time of the request, Complainant maintained only 25 cases—substantially below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below her typical historical caseload
- Reassignment constitutes an accommodation of last resort, available only when an employee cannot meet essential job functions
- Complainant failed to demonstrate inability to perform essential functions

The record reflected that Complainant's 2018 request for reduced inventory stated she desired approximately 38-40 cases, yet her contemporaneous caseload of 25 cases already fell below this threshold.

**Approval of Printer Accommodation**

The Agency approved Complainant's request for assistance printing and mailing correspondence. To address her physical limitations, management approved a small, portable printer that Complainant could operate. While awaiting delivery, management agreed to print and mail Complainant's correspondence.

However, before the printer's delivery, Complainant cancelled the order, stating she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Complainant later asserted she would be unable to lift either the portable printer or its paper—a position inconsistent with her earlier request for the device. Management continued to print and mail Complainant's letters notwithstanding the cancellation.

**Reconsideration and Appeal**

On July 12, 2021, Complainant appealed the denial of her reconsideration request. The Director of Collection Operations denied the appeal on August 24, 2021, reiterating that Complainant had rejected the Agency's offer of a lightweight portable printer and noting that she already maintained a reduced workload and was capable of performing essential job functions.

## Claim 5 – Denial of Official Time (October 26, 2021)

On October 20, 2021, Complainant requested official time to complete an affidavit in response to an EEO Investigator's request. The Agency granted Complainant:

- Six hours of official time on October 20, 2021
- Four hours of official time on October 21, 2021
- Additional official time approved on October 25, 2021

Despite receiving approximately 18 hours of official time, Complainant did not complete her affidavit. On October 26, 2021, Complainant requested additional official time, stating she had two questions remaining on the affidavit.

Supervisor1 denied this request based on: (1) the substantial official time already provided (approximately 18 hours); and (2) OCRD's instruction that Complainant contact the investigator directly to request an extension of her deadline if additional time was needed. The record indicates that Complainant's previous official time was partially devoted to information and documentation she had previously submitted in earlier complaints.

## Administrative Judge Determination

The EEOC Administrative Judge issued a summary judgment decision finding:

1. **No Hostile Work Environment**: The alleged incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute a hostile work environment. Complainant failed to establish that conduct was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus.

2. **No Comparative Evidence of Discrimination**: Complainant did not identify similarly situated employees outside her protected classes who received more favorable treatment regarding FMLA leave, case reassignments, or other employment decisions.

3. **Leave Claims**: The Agency properly maintained records of Complainant's leave balances. Upon Complainant's belated request for an audit, any discrepancies were corrected and Complainant received all paid leave to which she was entitled.

4. **Case Reassignment**: The reassignment of cases from the retired employee was appropriate, based on grade level, skill level, and Complainant's unusually low existing workload. Cases were distributed equitably among three similarly situated GS-12 employees.

5. **Reasonable Accommodations**: The Agency met its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act by:
   - Conducting an interactive meeting
   - Offering a lightweight portable printer accommodation
   - Arranging for management to print and mail correspondence during the interim period
   - Maintaining a caseload already below typical levels for Complainant's position

   Complainant's admission that her impairment did not limit essential job functions, combined with her rejection of offered accommodations, negated any violation.

6. **Official Time**: Eighteen hours of official time was objectively reasonable for completing an affidavit. The Agency's direction that Complainant request additional time directly from the investigator, consistent with OCRD guidance, was appropriate.

## Conclusion

The record supports the Administrative Judge's determination that Complainant failed to establish discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment based on disability or prior protected EEO activity. The Agency's personnel decisions were supported by legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons documented in the record.

# FINDINGS

## A. Jurisdiction and Allegations

The complainant, employed as a Carrier Technician at the Agency's Garland-South Station in Garland, Texas, filed an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint on April 17, 2021, alleging discrimination on the basis of disability (physical—neck and shoulder). The complaint encompassed nine distinct incidents occurring between November 7, 2020, and April 15, 2021, including allegations of harassment regarding work restrictions, required performance of duties outside medical limitations, public reprimand, denial of paid time to obtain required medical documentation, route reassignments, medical document review, referral to the District Reasonable Accommodation Committee (DRAC), denial of approved leave resulting in Absent Without Leave (AWOL) charges, and inadequate workplace accommodations.

## B. Jurisdictional Issues

The Agency dismissed one claim alleging that complainant was attacked by a dog while on duty and not properly compensated for missed time as a collateral attack on the Office of Workers' Compensation Programs (OWCP). This dismissal was affirmed as appropriate. The Commission has established that the EEO process cannot be used to challenge actions occurring during the OWCP adjudicatory process, as OWCP possesses exclusive jurisdiction over work-related injury compensation matters.

## C. Core Allegations

The remaining allegations constitute claims of discrimination and harassment based on disability under the Rehabilitation Act. Complainant alleged that the Manager of Customer Service subjected her to harassment based on her disability, required her to work outside her medical restrictions, charged her AWOL despite a previously approved leave request, and denied her necessary workplace accommodations in the form of a mail cart.

## D. Procedural Disposition

Following completion of the investigation and provision of the Report of Investigation to complainant, an administrative hearing was scheduled before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge. The Administrative Judge denied the hearing request as a sanction for complainant's failure to submit required Preliminary Case Information and failure to respond to an Order to Show Cause. The matter was remanded to the Agency, which issued a final decision concluding that complainant failed to prove the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

# FINDINGS

## Background

Complainant was employed as a Full-time Mail Handler Equipment Operator at the Agency's Morgan Processing and Distribution Center facility in New York, New York. On November 18, 2021, she filed an EEO complaint alleging discrimination on the bases of sex (female), disability (physical), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII and the Rehabilitation Act. The allegations included: (1) denial of overtime work within her limitations beginning June 25, 2021; (2) verbal abuse by a coworker on July 19, 2021, with no corrective action; (3) micromanagement and restricted work assignments beginning August 1, 2021; and (4) denial of a temporary schedule change request on August 31, 2021.

## Investigation and Transmission of ROI

The Agency conducted an investigation into the complaint. On April 5, 2022, the Agency transmitted the Report of Investigation (ROI) to Complainant and her non-attorney representative via email, stating that the copy would be available for download for 30 days. However, the record reflects that the destination server did not send a delivery notification confirming receipt. On the same date, the Agency provided additional documents for inclusion in the investigative file, including an Acting Supervisor's affidavit dated March 28, 2022, in which the Acting Supervisor stated he had no organizational relationship to Complainant at the relevant time and was not present on July 20, 2021.

On May 17, 2022, the Agency again emailed Complainant and her representative with notice that an electronic copy of the ROI would be available for download for 30 days. Again, the destination server did not send a delivery notification.

## Complainant's Response and Case Closure

On May 18, 2022, Complainant contacted an EEO Services Analyst by telephone to dispute the Acting Supervisor's affidavit. During this conversation, the Analyst informed Complainant that her case had been closed on May 1, 2022. Complainant questioned how her case could be closed without proper notification or receipt of the ROI. The Analyst advised Complainant that she could request a hearing and suggested she attach a letter explaining when she learned of the case closure.

On May 31, 2022, Complainant mailed a hearing request to both the Agency and the Commission's New York District Office. The Agency received and stamped the hearing request as received on June 6, 2022. Complainant's accompanying May 28, 2022, letter requested refutation of the Acting Supervisor's affidavit and asked for copies of his Employee Everything Report.

On June 2, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision, citing 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b) and concluding that Complainant failed to request a hearing within the required timeframe under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove the alleged discrimination.

## Subsequent Proceedings

The EEOC's New York District Office received Complainant's hearing request on June 10, 2022, and docketed it as Hearing No. 520-2022-00326X. On June 15, 2022, Complainant filed an appeal of the Agency's final decision.

On July 6, 2022, the Agency provided an updated affidavit from the Acting Supervisor, dated June 7, 2022. This updated affidavit contradicted the March 28, 2022, affidavit, stating that the Acting Supervisor's organizational relationship to Complainant during the complaint timeframe was Acting Supervisor. He reiterated that he was not present during the July 19, 2021, incident and stated he did not know whether Complainant or anyone acting on her behalf reported the harassment.

On November 29, 2022, an EEOC Administrative Judge issued an order dismissing Complainant's hearing request on the grounds that the Agency had already issued a final decision, which Complainant had appealed.

The EEOC's New York District Office received Complainant's hearing request on June 10, 2022, and docketed it as Hearing No. 520-2022-00326X. On June 15, 2022, Complainant filed an appeal of the Agency's final decision.

On July 6, 2022, the Agency provided an updated affidavit from the Acting Supervisor, dated June 7, 2022. This updated affidavit contradicted the March 28, 2022, affidavit, stating that the Acting Supervisor's organizational relationship to Complainant during the complaint timeframe was Acting Supervisor. He reiterated that he was not present during the July 19, 2021, incident and stated he did not know whether Complainant or anyone acting on her behalf reported the harassment.

On November 29, 2022, an EEOC Administrative Judge issued an order dismissing Complainant's hearing request on the grounds that the Agency had already issued a final decision, which Complainant had appealed.

# FINDINGS

## Overview
This investigative report examines five claims of age discrimination and harassment filed by Complainant, a Level 1 City Carrier at the Agency's Meadow Mesa Station facility in North Las Vegas, Nevada, alleging discriminatory treatment based on his age (born 1973). The investigation produced documentary evidence, affidavits, and statements from involved parties regarding events occurring between August 30, 2022, and November 1, 2022.

## Claim 1: Emergency Placement on August 30, 2022

**Complainant's Account:**
Complainant stated that he requested his supervisor (S1) sign or initial a union time request. When S1 indicated she would do so later and instructed him to return to work, Complainant questioned why he was being held to policy while S1 was not. The Postmaster (PM) subsequently intervened and, after an alleged confrontational exchange in the locker room involving raised voices and physical intimidation, demanded Complainant's badge and ordered him to vacate the premises. Complainant was placed on Emergency Placement (EP) in off-duty status without pay. Complainant asserted his age was a factor, claiming he was subjected to overburdened work assignments and constant unfavorable comparisons to younger carriers.

**Agency's Account:**
PM stated he observed Complainant engaging in time-wasting practices and failing to follow instructions in accordance with Agency policy, which precipitated the EP placement. PM denied the intimidation allegations, asserting he maintains distance from employees due to COVID precautions. S1 confirmed she instructed Complainant multiple times to deliver his route, noting he became argumentative with PM and failed to comply with her directives. S1 stated she had no knowledge of alleged locker room conduct. Both PM and S1 indicated that union steward consultation was unavailable at the time of departure and Complainant was instructed to contact the union after leaving the premises.

**Investigative Findings:**
Complainant provided no specific examples of similarly situated younger employees treated more favorably under comparable circumstances. The evidence established that management observed time-wasting conduct and directive non-compliance prior to the EP placement. While Complainant disputed the characterization of events, the factual predicate for the disciplinary action—failure to follow instructions—remained substantially undisputed.

## Claim 2: Suspension on September 14, 2022

**Complainant's Account:**
Complainant alleged he was suspended for failing to fasten his seatbelt before starting the vehicle engine and for exiting the vehicle while the engine remained running. Complainant stated he requested a union steward but was denied. Complainant asserted the discipline violated Agency policy as outlined in Handbook M-41, Section 812, which requires seatbelts be worn while the vehicle is in motion, not necessarily before engine ignition.

**Agency's Account:**
S2 stated he observed Complainant exit the mail truck and walk in front of it while the engine was operating—a safety violation. S2 affirmed that Agency policy mandates seatbelt use at all times while operating a vehicle. S2 indicated that due to the immediate EP placement, union contact was required to occur off postal property. S1 stated she was not present during the incident and had no direct knowledge of the occurrence.

**Investigative Findings:**
The record reflects that a Notice of 14-Day Suspension was issued on September 22, 2022, citing the August 30, 2022, failure to follow instructions as the basis for suspension rather than the seatbelt incident. The seatbelt incident served as grounds for the September 14 EP placement. Complainant did not assert that age was a contributing factor to this incident and provided no comparative examples of younger employees treated more favorably. The safety violation itself—operating a vehicle without a seatbelt fastened—was substantiated and remained undisputed.

## Claim 3: Bathroom Confrontation on September 20, 2022

**Complainant's Account:**
Complainant alleged that S2 followed him into the bathroom on two separate occasions on September 20, 2022, yelled at him, and threatened disciplinary action. Complainant attributed this conduct to his age, theorizing that supervisors subjected him to heightened scrutiny due to increased bathroom frequency associated with aging.

**Agency's Account:**
S2 denied raising his voice and stated that if he followed Complainant, it was due to performance concerns. S2 indicated that rather than conducting bathroom business, Complainant spent extended periods in the locker room and appeared to be accessing his locker. S1 stated she had no knowledge of incidents occurring in the bathroom.

**Investigative Findings:**
The accounts of the bathroom incidents directly conflict. The investigation produced no corroborating evidence of the alleged yelling or threats. Complainant offered no specific comparable examples of younger employees who engaged in similar extended locker room activities yet escaped supervisory scrutiny. The assertion that age-related physiological changes prompted discriminatory treatment remained speculative and unsupported by evidence of differential treatment of younger employees.

## Claim 4: Seatbelt Confrontation on September 24, 2022

**Complainant's Account:**
Complainant stated that S2 yelled at him for failing to fasten his seatbelt before starting the engine. Complainant asserted that S2 misinterpreted Agency policy, citing Handbook M-41, Section 812, which requires seatbelts be fastened before the vehicle is placed in motion, not necessarily before engine start. Complainant further stated he contacted the National Association of Letter Carriers (NALC) office, which confirmed his interpretation. Complainant asserted that S1 subsequently told him to follow supervisor instructions and fasten his seatbelt before starting the engine.

**Agency's Account:**
S2 stated he initially believed seatbelts must be fastened before engine start. S2 indicated he thereafter contacted safety personnel and was informed that no written Agency policy specified this requirement. S2 stated he communicated this information to Complainant, who was then permitted to proceed with his route. S1 confirmed that S2 requested her assessment of Complainant's conduct; she observed no violation. S1 indicated she subsequently directed Complainant to follow supervisor instructions regarding seatbelt fastening, though she expressed uncertainty as to whether the requirement was uniformly applied across all carriers.

**Investigative Findings:**
The evidence reveals disagreement regarding the correct interpretation of the seatbelt policy and confusion among supervisors regarding its application. However, S2 clarified the matter with safety personnel, and Complainant was afforded the opportunity to continue his route. Complainant did not assert that age was a factor in this incident and provided no examples of younger employees treated differently regarding policy interpretation or supervisory directives.

## Claim 5: Escort from Premises on November 1, 2022

**Complainant's Account:**
Complainant presented S1 with a doctor's note restricting him from overtime due to repetitive motion pain in his right shoulder. Complainant alleged S1 refused to honor the medical restriction and demanded he continue delivering until his route was completed. When Complainant expressed concern that working overtime contradicted medical guidance, S1 demanded his badge and he was escorted from the premises. Complainant was placed on EP, effective November 2, 2022. Complainant attributed this action to age, asserting that as an older worker, he recovers more slowly from injuries and should not be subjected to tasks contradicting medical restrictions.

**Agency's Account:**
S1 stated that Complainant indicated, based on union guidance, that he could return undelivered mail and was not required to follow management directives. S1 asserted she requested three times that Complainant finish his route. S1 indicated she submitted Complainant's medical documentation to Occupational Health Management (OHM) for guidance. S1 stated that OHM advised her that Complainant could complete his route that day and that OHM would provide guidance on whether the doctor's note constituted a limited duty job offer or required formal light duty request submission to the PM.

**Investigative Findings:**
The evidence indicates a dispute regarding the applicability and priority of the medical restriction relative to work directives. S1 followed established protocol by submitting the medical documentation to OHM, which advised that Complainant could complete his route pending further guidance on the formal classification of the restriction. Complainant did not dispute that he refused to follow S1's instructions but asserted the instructions were unsafe given medical constraints. Complainant provided no examples of younger employees with medical restrictions who were treated more favorably or exempted from work assignments pending OHM review. While disability concerns may be implicated, Complainant did not raise disability as a basis for his EEO complaint.

## Summary of Investigation Results

Across all five claims, the investigation established:

1. Complainant was observed engaging in conduct the Agency characterized as policy violations and work performance deficiencies.
2. Complainant did not dispute the underlying factual predicates for disciplinary actions (time-wasting, failure to follow instructions, seatbelt violations, refusal to complete assigned work).
3. No documentary evidence of age-related comments by management was identified.
4. Complainant provided no specific examples of similarly situated younger employees who received more favorable treatment under comparable circumstances.
5. Management's stated justifications for each action were grounded in workplace conduct, safety policy, and work performance rather than age-related considerations.

The AJ found that these predicates, which Complainant did not dispute, provided sufficient nondiscriminatory justification for the discipline and other actions management meted out. The AJ found that Complainant did not offer evidence that management made biased comments about his age or that they treated younger workers more favorably. As a result, the AJ found that no reasonable factfinder, even viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to Complainant, could conclude the Agency's actions were tainted by considerations of Complainant's age. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s decision. The instant appeal from Complainant followed.

# FINDINGS

## Overview
This investigative report examines five claims of age discrimination and harassment filed by Complainant, a Level 1 City Carrier at the Agency's Meadow Mesa Station facility in North Las Vegas, Nevada, alleging discriminatory treatment based on his age (born 1973). The investigation produced documentary evidence, affidavits, and statements from involved parties regarding events occurring between August 31, 2022, and November 1, 2022.

## Claim 1: Emergency Placement on August 30, 2022

**Complainant's Account:**
Complainant stated that he requested his supervisor (S1) sign or initial a union time request. When S1 indicated she would do so later and instructed him to return to work, Complainant questioned why he was being held to policy while S1 was not. The Postmaster (PM) subsequently intervened and, after an alleged confrontational exchange in the locker room involving raised voices and physical intimidation, demanded Complainant's badge and ordered him to vacate the premises. Complainant was placed on Emergency Placement (EP) in off-duty status without pay. Complainant asserted his age was a factor, claiming he was subjected to overburdened work assignments and constant unfavorable comparisons to younger carriers.

**Agency's Account:**
PM stated he observed Complainant engaging in time-wasting practices and failing to follow instructions in accordance with Agency policy, which precipitated the EP placement. PM denied the intimidation allegations, asserting he maintains distance from employees due to COVID precautions. S1 confirmed she instructed Complainant multiple times to deliver his route, noting he became argumentative with PM and failed to comply with her directives. S1 stated she had no knowledge of alleged locker room conduct. Both PM and S1 indicated that union steward consultation was unavailable at the time of departure and Complainant was instructed to contact the union after leaving the premises.

**Investigative Findings:**
Complainant provided no specific examples of similarly situated younger employees treated more favorably under comparable circumstances. The evidence established that management observed time-wasting conduct and directive non-compliance prior to the EP placement. While Complainant disputed the characterization of events, the factual predicate for the disciplinary action—failure to follow instructions—remained substantially undisputed.

## Claim 2: Suspension on September 14, 2022

**Complainant's Account:**
Complainant alleged he was suspended for failing to fasten his seatbelt before starting the vehicle engine and for exiting the vehicle while the engine remained running. Complainant stated he requested a union steward but was denied. Complainant asserted the discipline violated Agency policy as outlined in Handbook M-41, Section 812, which requires seatbelts be worn while the vehicle is in motion, not necessarily before engine ignition.

**Agency's Account:**
S2 stated he observed Complainant exit the mail truck and walk in front of it while the engine was operating—a safety violation. S2 affirmed that Agency policy mandates seatbelt use at all times while operating a vehicle. S2 indicated that due to the immediate EP placement, union contact was required to occur off postal property. S1 stated she was not present during the incident and had no direct knowledge of the occurrence.

**Investigative Findings:**
The record reflects that a Notice of 14-Day Suspension was issued on September 22, 2022, citing the August 30, 2022, failure to follow instructions as the basis for suspension rather than the seatbelt incident. The seatbelt incident served as grounds for the September 14 EP placement. Complainant did not assert that age was a contributing factor to this incident and provided no comparative examples of younger employees treated more favorably. The safety violation itself—operating a vehicle without a seatbelt fastened—was substantiated and remained undisputed.

## Claim 3: Bathroom Confrontation on September 20, 2022

**Complainant's Account:**
Complainant alleged that S2 followed him into the bathroom on two separate occasions on September 20, 2022, yelled at him, and threatened disciplinary action. Complainant attributed this conduct to his age, theorizing that supervisors subjected him to heightened scrutiny due to increased bathroom frequency associated with aging.

**Agency's Account:**
S2 denied raising his voice and stated that if he followed Complainant, it was due to performance concerns. S2 indicated that rather than conducting bathroom business, Complainant spent extended periods in the locker room and appeared to be accessing his locker. S1 stated she had no knowledge of incidents occurring in the bathroom.

**Investigative Findings:**
The accounts of the bathroom incidents directly conflict. The investigation produced no corroborating evidence of the alleged yelling or threats. Complainant offered no specific comparable examples of younger employees who engaged in similar extended locker room activities yet escaped supervisory scrutiny. The assertion that age-related physiological changes prompted discriminatory treatment remained speculative and unsupported by evidence of differential treatment of younger employees.

## Claim 4: Seatbelt Confrontation on September 24, 2022

**Complainant's Account:**
Complainant stated that S2 yelled at him for failing to fasten his seatbelt before starting the engine. Complainant asserted that S2 misinterpreted Agency policy, citing Handbook M-41, Section 812, which requires seatbelts be fastened before the vehicle is placed in motion, not necessarily before engine start. Complainant further stated he contacted the National Association of Letter Carriers (NALC) office, which confirmed his interpretation. Complainant asserted that S1 subsequently told him to follow supervisor instructions and fasten his seatbelt before starting the engine.

**Agency's Account:**
S2 stated he initially believed seatbelts must be fastened before engine start. S2 indicated he thereafter contacted safety personnel and was informed that no written Agency policy specified this requirement. S2 stated he communicated this information to Complainant, who was then permitted to proceed with his route. S1 confirmed that S2 requested her assessment of Complainant's conduct; she observed no violation. S1 indicated she subsequently directed Complainant to follow supervisor instructions regarding seatbelt fastening, though she expressed uncertainty as to whether the requirement was uniformly applied across all carriers.

**Investigative Findings:**
The evidence reveals disagreement regarding the correct interpretation of the seatbelt policy and confusion among supervisors regarding its application. However, S2 clarified the matter with safety personnel, and Complainant was afforded the opportunity to continue his route. Complainant did not assert that age was a factor in this incident and provided no examples of younger employees treated differently regarding policy interpretation or supervisory directives.

## Claim 5: Escort from Premises on November 1, 2022

**Complainant's Account:**
Complainant presented S1 with a doctor's note restricting him from overtime due to repetitive motion pain in his right shoulder. Complainant alleged S1 refused to honor the medical restriction and demanded he continue delivering until his route was completed. When Complainant expressed concern that working overtime contradicted medical guidance, S1 demanded his badge and he was escorted from the premises. Complainant was placed on EP, effective November 2, 2022. Complainant attributed this action to age, asserting that as an older worker, he recovers more slowly from injuries and should not be subjected to tasks contradicting medical restrictions.

**Agency's Account:**
S1 stated that Complainant indicated, based on union guidance, that he could return undelivered mail and was not required to follow management directives. S1 asserted she requested three times that Complainant finish his route. S1 indicated she submitted Complainant's medical documentation to Occupational Health Management (OHM) for guidance. S1 stated that OHM advised her that Complainant could complete his route that day and that OHM would provide guidance on whether the doctor's note constituted a limited duty job offer or required formal light duty request submission to the PM.

**Investigative Findings:**
The evidence indicates a dispute regarding the applicability and priority of the medical restriction relative to work directives. S1 followed established protocol by submitting the medical documentation to OHM, which advised that Complainant could complete his route pending further guidance on the formal classification of the restriction. Complainant did not dispute that he refused to follow S1's instructions but asserted the instructions were unsafe given medical constraints. Complainant provided no examples of younger employees with medical restrictions who were treated more favorably or exempted from work assignments pending OHM review. While disability concerns may be implicated, Complainant did not raise disability as a basis for his EEO complaint.

## Summary of Investigation Results

Across all five claims, the investigation established:

1. Complainant was observed engaging in conduct the Agency characterized as policy violations and work performance deficiencies.
2. Complainant did not dispute the underlying factual predicates for disciplinary actions (time-wasting, failure to follow instructions, seatbelt violations, refusal to complete assigned work).
3. No documentary evidence of age-related comments by management was identified.
4. Complainant provided no specific examples of similarly situated younger employees who received more favorable treatment under comparable circumstances.
5. Management's stated justifications for each action were grounded in workplace conduct, safety policy, and work performance rather than age-related considerations.

# FINDINGS

## Background and Jurisdiction

The Complainant, a PSE Sales and Services Distribution Associate, Grade Level 06 P, employed at the Agency's Cape Central Post Office in Cape Coral, Florida, filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint on April 4, 2022. The complaint alleged that she was subjected to ongoing racial harassment during the period of late January through early March 2022. Specifically, Complainant claimed that her first-line supervisor, who is African American, made racial slurs, made offensive statements referencing slavery, and threatened to physically assault her. Complainant further alleged that when she reported these incidents to management officials, no action was taken. Complainant initially included a retaliation claim but withdrew it during the investigation. The Agency conducted an investigation and subsequently issued a final decision finding no discrimination or unlawful retaliation. Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge but failed to comply with procedural orders and was dismissed from the hearing process.

## Factual Findings

**Complainant's Account of Alleged Incidents:**

Complainant alleged that between late January and early March 2022, her supervisor made the following statements and threats:
- Late January/early February 2022: When asked about inputting hours into the computer, Supervisor allegedly responded, "I'll slap the shit out of you."
- When asked about taking a break, Supervisor allegedly stated, "people shouldn't be allowed breaks, Black people used to be slaves."
- February 3, 2022: When Complainant asked for clarification, Supervisor allegedly threatened, "I'll slap the shit out of you if you don't catch on."
- February 5, 2022: Regarding a heavy package, Supervisor allegedly responded, "full of shit. You can't lift that?"
- February 8, 2022: When instructed to bring wagons around, Supervisor allegedly stated, "You need to do it because you're White..."
- February 24, 2022: When Complainant said "huh?" after not hearing Supervisor, he allegedly responded, "What do you mean huh? I'll slap the shit out of you."
- March 3, 2022: Upon observing Complainant exit the housekeeping closet, Supervisor allegedly stated, "White people don't steal, they buy their own shit."

Complainant asserted that she reported these incidents to the Manager, Customer Service, and to the union, but no action was taken.

**Supervisor's Response:**

The Supervisor unequivocally denied making any of the statements attributed to him. He stated that he believed he and Complainant had a good working relationship until the formal complaint was filed.

**Manager's Statement:**

The Manager affirmatively stated that Complainant never reported to her any of the comments allegedly made by Supervisor.

**Corroborating Witness:**

Another supervisor (Supervisor 2) recalled that Complainant once mentioned that Supervisor told her he would "slap her upside the head." However, Supervisor 2 did not corroborate any of the alleged racial statements. He stated that he advised Complainant to report the matter to the Manager and that Complainant indicated she did not wish to file such a report.

**Post-Investigation Actions:**

Following the Agency's investigation and final decision, the Agency apparently reassigned Complainant to a different supervisor. Complainant did not raise her reassignment as a claim in her complaint.

**Procedural History:**

After receiving notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge, Complainant requested a hearing. However, she failed to comply with the Administrative Judge's October 24, 2022 order to submit preliminary case information and did not appear at the initial conference scheduled for November 24, 2022. On January 19, 2023, the Administrative Judge dismissed Complainant's hearing request and remanded the complaint to the Agency for a final decision.

## Conclusion Regarding Credibility and Evidence

The record reflects material contradictions between Complainant's allegations and the testimony of those who would have observed or been informed of the alleged conduct. The Manager's denial that Complainant ever reported the alleged incidents to her is particularly significant, given Complainant's explicit claim of having done so. While Supervisor 2 provided limited corroboration regarding a threat to "slap," he did not corroborate any of the racial statements central to Complainant's claim and testified that Complainant declined to pursue a formal report with management. The Supervisor's categorical denial, coupled with his assertion of a positive working relationship prior to the complaint, further undercuts Complainant's account. The lack of documentary evidence, corroborating witnesses to the specific incidents alleged, and the contradictions between Complainant's account and management's account of whether the incidents were reported create substantial questions regarding the factual basis for the harassment allegations.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail Processing Clerk at the Agency’s Atlanta Processing and Distribution Center in Atlanta, Georgia. Complainant stated that she had previously filed an EEO complaint in September 2018, which remained pending before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) at the time of her affidavit for the instant EEO complaint. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 97. She explained that she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression as a result of an incident where she was sexually harassed by a co-worker (the subject of her prior complaint), and that she also suffers from back, foot, and knee issues so she is unable to stand or walk for extended periods of time, cannot climb or descend stairs, and has restrictions on bending, stooping, and lifting. See ROI at 97-98. She also stated that due to the PTSD she suffers as a result of the co-worker’s sexual assault, her doctor stated that she can no longer work in the same facility as the co-worker who assaulted her. See ROI at 98-99. Complainant explained that the sexual harassment/assault occurred in September 2019 after which she went on Family & Medical Leave Act (FMLA) leave. See ROI at 100. She stated that she was released to return to work at a different facility from her harasser in April 2020, but when she arrived at work, her harasser was still there. See ROI at 100. She further alleged that in June 2020, she suffered a knee injury in the workplace, and she submitted documents to the Agency pertaining to her knee injury in July 2020, but received no response. See ROI at 100. She stated that the Agency’s Reasonable Accommodation Committee requested additional documentation which she had already provided and that they ignored her limitation resulting from her PTSD that required she be moved to a different facility from her harasser, instead focusing only on her physical restrictions due to her knee injury. See ROI at 100. She stated that in July 2021, she was finally given a modified assignment to a different location that accommodated her physical restrictions. 2 See ROI at 100. She went out on COVID leave on August 16, 2021, and then was later hospitalized for sepsis so she was ultimately not cleared to return to work until September 21, 2021. However, Complainant stated that she has not been returned to work because the Agency has refused to accommodate her restrictions, and she has only been told by management that there was no work available for her based on her restrictions. 3 See ROI at 100-105. There is no explanation or documentation in the record of Complainant’s new position or why it took the Agency a full year to move Complainant to a different work facility than her harasser. We emphasize that there is no statement from any Agency official confirming that any effort was made to accommodate Complainant’s restrictions from September 2021 onwards or that such an effort was unsuccessful. Complainant further alleged that she should not have been placed on leave without pay (LWOP) since November 21, 2021, because she was not able to work due to the Agency’s failure to accommodate her restrictions. In January 2022, she was denied a bid position, and the position was instead given to someone who had less seniority, while Complainant was marked “ineligible” with no explanation. 4 See ROI at 105; 108-9. EEO Complaint On May 13, 2022, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of race (African-American/Native American/Cuban), sex (female), color (Brown), disability (physical and mental), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 when: 1. Since November 10, 2021, she was not accommodated per her medical restrictions. 2. Since November 10, 2021, to present, she was charged LWOP. 3. On January 24, 2022, she was denied a bid position. 5 The Supervisor of Distribution Operations stated in her affidavit that Complainant’s bid was denied because she did not receive any updated medical documentation stating Complainant could fully perform her duties within 6 months. See ROI at 152. There is no evidence in the record indicating that Complainant was actually requested to provide such documentation or told she needed to do so as Complainant stated she was given no explanation for the denial. In addition, we note that the Collective Bargaining Agreement specifically states that in such a situation “management may, at the time of the submission of the bid or at any time thereafter, request that the employee provide medical certification indicating that the employee will be able to fully perform the duties of the bid for position within six months of the bid.” See ROI at 337. Complainant’s complaint also included three additional claims, specifically that between April 2020 and November 9, 2021, she was not accommodated per her medical restrictions; that on unspecified dates, her leave was not properly coded as workers’ compensation (OWCP) leave; and on unspecified dates, she was denied insurance benefits. Complainant had filed a motion to amend a pre-existing complaint to include her denial of reasonable accommodation claim for the period from April 2020 onwards but the AJ assigned to her other case denied the motion, finding that the denial of accommodation claim was not sufficiently like or related to her existing claim and noted that the time limits on EEO counseling be tolled from November 11, 2021, the date she filed the motion to amend. See ROI at 17-20. The Agency dismissed the denial of reasonable accommodation claim for the dates prior to November 10, 2021, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(1) because of untimely counselor contact. See ROI at 62-63. The Agency also dismissed the claims regarding her leave not being properly coded and the denial of insurance benefits as collateral attacks on the workers’ compensation adjudicatory process. See ROI at 63-65. We find that the Agency’s affirmance of the claims regarding Complainant’s leave not being properly coded as OWCP leave and the denial of insurance benefits were On December 6, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency found that Complainant did not submit required medical documentation to support her request for a reasonable accommodation or to show that she could perform the positions of her bid position within six months. The Agency also determined that Complainant did not demonstrate pretext for discrimination. The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

# FINDINGS

## Background and Complainant's Medical Conditions

At the time of the events at issue, Complainant was employed as a Mail Processing Clerk at the Agency's Atlanta Processing and Distribution Center. Complainant suffers from multiple documented medical conditions, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression resulting from sexual harassment and assault by a co-worker, as well as physical limitations affecting her back, feet, and knees that prevent extended standing or walking, stair navigation, and bending, stooping, or lifting activities.

## Prior Sexual Harassment and Delayed Accommodation

Complainant was sexually harassed and assaulted by a co-worker in September 2019. Following this incident, she was placed on FMLA leave. Medical documentation indicated that due to her PTSD, Complainant's physician stated she could no longer work in the same facility as her harasser. Although Complainant was released to return to work at a different facility in April 2020, her harasser remained at her original facility, preventing her requested accommodation.

## Workplace Injury and Lack of Response

In June 2020, Complainant sustained a workplace knee injury and submitted related documentation to the Agency in July 2020. The Agency's Reasonable Accommodation Committee requested additional documentation that Complainant had already provided and focused solely on her physical restrictions rather than addressing her documented medical need to be separated from her harasser.

## Delayed Accommodation and Subsequent Medical Events

Approximately one year after her initial injury, in July 2021, Complainant was assigned to a modified position at a different location accommodating her physical restrictions. No explanation or documentation exists in the record regarding the specifics of this new position or the justification for the year-long delay. Complainant went on COVID leave on August 16, 2021, and was subsequently hospitalized for sepsis, ultimately not cleared to return to work until September 21, 2021.

## Failure to Accommodate Post-Return

items.source: During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as a Taxpayer Advocate in Laguna Niguel, California. On November 4, 2021, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on race (Hispanic) and national origin (Mexican). By letter dated November 16, 2021, the Agency accepted the formal complaint for investigation and framed the claims in the following fashion: Whether a co-worker who was an On-the-Job Instructor (OJI), as well as a Lead, subjected Complainant to harassment based on her race/national origin (Hispanic/Mexican) on multiple occasions beginning in June 2020 and continuing through July 2021 when, among other matters, the OJI/Lead: 1. Made fun of Complainant’s accent and said she disliked speaking to Complainant. 2. Tried to sabotage Complainant’s work by creating a list of inventory late actions and expired casework, and purposely gave Complainant misinformation regarding how to process cases. 3. Filled Complainant’s calendar with unrealistic appointments that not even experienced employees could complete. 4. Advised Complainant’s manager to have Complainant process a fraudulent tax return. After an investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination. Specifically, the Agency determined that “assuming [Complainant’s initial supervisor, S1] made these and other similar comments [as set forth in incident (1)], the statements would be unwelcome verbal conduct based on Complainant’s protected categories of race/national origin/ethnicity.” Final Agency Decision (FAD) at 12. However, the Agency, in its final decision, further set forth that: Complainant has produced no persuasive evidence that management’s actions described in [alleged incidents] 2, 3, and 4 were harassment based on her statutorily protected classes. Complainant’s uncorroborated statements that management was motivated by race/ethnicity and/or national origin to take the actions complained of are not sufficient to sustain her burden of showing harassment…Finally, we note that Complainant’s allegations of harassment were addressed through an internal anti-harassment inquiry, which did not substantiate Complainant’s claims.” FAD at 13. The instant appeal followed. Complainant asserts that the Agency’s final decision did not properly set forth that the alleged harasser was initially her former manager (prior to serving as her Lead and OJI). Complainant reiterates that S1 made derogatory comments regarding her accent since her first day of employment. Complainant asserts that she provided notice to S2 regarding S1’s behavior and requested a change of supervisor, but that S2 ignored the harassment and allowed the behavior to continue. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision finding no discrimination. The Agency reiterates that Complainant failed to establish that she was subjected to harassment. Regarding the alleged comments made by S1 to Complainant regarding her accent, the Agency sets forth that “[a]ssuming the truth of Complainant’s allegations, nothing in S1’s comments indicate she mocked Complainant’s accent or that the comments were based on her being of Mexican descent. At best, [S1] indicated she expressed difficulty in communicating with Complainant. At worst, S1’s comments were the type of insensitive, hurtful comments that the Commission has declined to find as discriminatory.” Agency Response Brief at 11. The Agency asserts that Complainant’s claims fall short of the severity and pervasiveness required for a hostile work environment. Furthermore, the Agency states that management promptly separated Complainant and S1. Specifically, the Agency states that after Complainant raised the issue of harassment by S1 in late July 2021, S4 separated Complainant and S1 and that Complainant set forth that she had no further contact with S1 after this separation. The Agency further sets forth regarding Complainant raising the matter of alleged harassment by S1 with S2, it “appears” that Complainant only expressed a “lack of support.” Agency Response Brief at 17- 18.

# FINDINGS

## A. Jurisdiction and Timeliness

The Agency properly accepted Complainant's formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed on November 4, 2021, and framed the allegations within the statutory framework of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The complaint alleged discrimination based on race (Hispanic) and national origin (Mexican). The Agency conducted an investigation and issued a Final Agency Decision (FAD) on an unspecified date. Complainant timely appealed the FAD to the Commission.

## B. Factual Summary

Complainant worked as a Taxpayer Advocate in Laguna Niguel, California, during the period at issue (June 2020 through July 2021). Complainant alleged that a co-worker who served as an On-the-Job Instructor (OJI) and Lead (hereafter "S1") subjected her to harassment based on her Hispanic race and Mexican national origin. The alleged harassing conduct included: (1) comments regarding Complainant's accent and statements that S1 disliked speaking with Complainant; (2) attempts to sabotage Complainant's work through misinformation and the creation of detrimental case lists; (3) scheduling unrealistic appointments incompletable by experienced employees; and (4) advice to Complainant's manager to have Complainant process fraudulent tax returns.

Complainant further alleged that she reported the harassment to her manager (S2) and requested a change of supervisor, but that S2 failed to address the conduct. In late July 2021, after Complainant raised the harassment issue, management separated Complainant and S1. Complainant confirmed that she had no further contact with S1 following this separation.

## C. Agency's Finding of No Discrimination

The Agency's investigation resulted in a finding of no discrimination. Regarding Complainant's accent-related allegations, the Agency concluded that assuming the truth of Complainant's allegations, the comments were, at worst, "insensitive, hurtful comments" that did not constitute discriminatory conduct. The Agency determined that Complainant failed to establish that S1's comments mocked her accent or were based on her Mexican descent; rather, the comments merely reflected S1's expressed difficulty in communicating with Complainant.

Regarding allegations 2, 3, and 4, the Agency found that Complainant produced no persuasive evidence that management's actions were harassment based on her protected classes. The Agency concluded that Complainant's uncorroborated assertions that S1 was motivated by race or national origin were insufficient to sustain her burden of proof. The Agency further noted that Complainant's allegations had been addressed through an internal anti-harassment inquiry that did not substantiate her claims.

The Agency emphasized that management promptly addressed the harassment complaint by separating Complainant and S1 in late July 2021.
