items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-15, Primary Care Physician, at the Agency’s East Orange Veterans Affairs Medical Center in East Orange, New Jersey. 1. She was denied her repeated request for reasonable accommodation from April 21, 2020, to her termination on January 22, 2021; 2 and 2. She was charged as Absent Without Leave (AWOL) from August 10, 2020, to her termination on January 22, 2021. At the conclusion of the investigation, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). An investigator noted in the report of investigation that Complainant did not provide an affidavit requested during the investigation of the complaint. 3 The AJ issued a decision without holding a hearing, finding no discrimination. The record indicates that Complainant was appointed as a Primary Care Physician at the Agency on March 3, 2019, subject to a two-year probationary period. As a Primary Care Physician, Complainant’s essential duties included: interviewing and examining patients daily (typically 12), via in-person and virtual; examining patients who were present for face-to-face visits; documenting patient visits in the Agency’s electronic medical record; and ordering consults, labs, and medications using the electronic medical record. Complainant indicated that she sustained a shoulder injury on July 12, 2019. We note that Complainant did not claim that she notified her supervisors or requested a reasonable accommodation at the time of her July 12, 2019 injury. Complainant indicated that in December 2019, she aggravated a prior injury to her right shoulder and notified her supervisors of this December 2019 injury shortly thereafter. Complainant claimed that due to her physical conditions, she was unable to lift her right arm, use a mouse or keyboard, or write, and was therefore unable to perform physical examinations on patients, unable to document notes, or use a computer for more than a few minutes at a time. Regarding claim 1, Complainant’s supervisor (S1) indicated that he became aware of Complainant’s right shoulder condition in December 2019. S1 stated that on February 25, 2020, Complainant made a verbal reasonable accommodation request and submitted Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) requesting no lifting, no prolonged upper extremely fine manipulation with the right arm/hand, part-time, light duties to include 20 hours work week, no grabbing, and assistance with computer tasks as needed. Our records indicate that on August 2, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint, [number removed], regarding her January 22, 2021 termination, recommended by the Professional Standards Board. The Agency issued its final Agency decision finding no discrimination. Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision, and that matter is pending before the Commission, in EEOC [number removed]. The investigator noted that when asked on several occasions, Complainant stated that she sent her affidavit to a “higher authority.” Complainant’s affidavit was not included in the Report of Investigation. Complainant indicates that she sent her affidavit to then Secretary of the Agency, instead. The record indicates that Complainant provided the affidavit to the AJ. After being on leave since December 2019, due to her conditions, Complainant returned to work on March 2, 2020, with the work shift restrictions in place as she requested (i.e., work four hours per day and four hours Leave Without Pay (LWOP), five days per week). She was required to complete the Agency’s Talent Management System training modules online and see two or three patients by the end of the week if needed. Complainant failed to see a patient or complete the required training. A Medical Assistant reported that on March 4, 2020, Complainant declined to see a patient in the waiting room who had already waited several months to see her. Complainant told the Medical Assistant that she could not see the patient because her shoulder was bothering her, and she could barely hold a pen to write notes. On March 5, 2020, S1, Complainant’s second level supervisor (S2), and the Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator initiated an interactive process regarding Complainant’s accommodation request and held a meeting. During the meeting, Complainant made it clear that she could not perform patient examinations of her patients, was unable to complete patient paperwork, and was unable to use a computer for more than a few minutes at a time. Because there was concern even part-time work would worsen her condition, the Agency decided to grant Complainant’s alternative accommodation of continuing LWOP to rehabilitate her injury for a six-week period. Complainant indicated that she remained in an approved LWOP status from March 4, 2020, through August 10, 2020. Two weeks after the meeting, Complainant requested 100% telework. In response, on March 25, 2020, S1 requested Complainant provide physician documentation regarding her ability to perform essential functions of her position including her limitations with typing notes, placing orders including consults, sending out lab letters, and filling out paperwork and forms as requested by her patients. During this time period, due to COVID-19, non-urgent appointments were cancelled, and telework arrangements were made for hospital physicians on ad hoc basis, i.e., 50% telework alternating weeks in-person in the hospital and at-home teleworking. Meanwhile, the Agency prepared dictation software to be installed in Complainant’s computer (to minimize typing); two ergonomic chairs to be delivered to her office for each of her exam rooms; and an ergonomic mouse and keyboard were shipped to her home and a second set was delivered to her office. A laptop was approved on March 3, 2020, but the delivery was delayed due to a shortage of equipment. S1 sent a second laptop request through the Computer/Electronic Accommodation program (CAP), within the Department of Defense, to try to get one sooner but the CAP denied the request because during the “Needs Assessment,” Complainant failed to submit sufficient medical documentation to support the need for a second laptop, as well as a telework agreement. On June 2, 2020, the Agency secured a laptop for Complainant, but she never signed a telework agreement, i.e., addressing teleworking for one to three months due to her temporary disability. S1 indicated that the Agency could not offer Complainant’s requested unconditional 100% telework for at least a year because she failed to provide medical documentation to justify the request. Further, S1 stated that the hospital had a shortage of physicians, some providers were sick with COVID-19, and Complainant’s patients were being covered by other physicians. Thus, the Agency decided to offer Complainant a telework agreement for one to three months, dependent upon updates to her medical documentation. Complainant did not accept the Agency’s telework agreement. The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator indicated that Complainant made several accommodation requests, including one on April 21, 2020. Complainant requested 100% telework, 20 hours per work week, and modified work assignments for one year to permanent basis. The Coordinator stated, and the record reflects, that she made numerous requests, including several emails in June 2020, to Complainant for medical documentation of her disability in connection with her reasonable accommodation requests. Complainant failed to provide such documentation. Specifically, the Coordinator stated that Complainant was asked to provide medical documentations relating to the effectiveness of telework/telemedicine accommodation with her medical condition and the information relating to the duration of her medical condition, including her consent to contact her physician in order to proceed with her accommodation request. Complainant failed to provide such information. Thus, on August 7, 2020, the Coordinator closed Complainant’s request for reasonable accommodation and informed her that the case would be reopened if she provided the requested documentation. The record reflects that Complainant provided the Agency a copy of her doctor’s (DR1) Return to Work statements. In a Return to Work, dated January 13, 2020, DR1 indicated that Complainant was seen in his office on January 13, 2020, and may return to work after follow-up on February 10, 2020. In a Return to Work, dated February 10, 2020, DR1 indicated that Complainant was seen in his office on February 10, 2020, and may return to work on March 2, 2020. The record also reflects that Complainant provided a doctor’s (DR2) statement dated February 25, 2020. Therein, DR2 stated that Complainant was under DR2’s care for her right shoulder; she should be given light duty and part-time work with no lifting; she should be given assistance with computer tasks; and her return to full duty would be reevaluated in six weeks. In DR2’s statement, dated April 21, 2020, DR2 indicated that Complainant should be allowed to continue in light duty, work from home via laptop, and telemedicine; and her status to return to full duty would be reevaluated on May 19, 2020. In two statements, both dated May 19, 2020, DR2 stated that Complainant was evaluated on May 19, 2020, for right shoulder; she had dexterity issues; she was to continue in physical therapy to oversee shoulder exercises and working from home via telemedicine; she was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support; and her status to return to normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks. The record indicates that on July 15, 2020, Complainant submitted DR2’s statement dated June 22, 2020. Therein, DR2 stated that Complainant should be allowed to work from home via telemedicine, maximum 20 hours weekly; she was in pain with dexterity issues; she had issues with gripping and right arm/hand manipulation; she reported pain and issues with gripping the wheel when driving; she would continue with physical therapy to oversee shoulder exercises; she was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support; and her status to resume normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks. In a statement dated July 30, 2020, DR2, reiterating the foregoing statement, indicated that he was recommending an evaluation with a back specialist for Complainant’s condition; her status to return would be reevaluated; and her “shoulder symptoms are well controlled and is discharged at this time.” Regarding claim 2, S1 and S2 indicated that after Complainant’s reasonable accommodation case was closed, the Coordinator suggested it was reasonable to charge Complainant AWOL for her absence. Considering the Coordinator’s suggestion and the fact that Complainant had not worked for nearly eight months without providing medical documentation as requested, management decided to place her in AWOL starting August 10, 2020. The Agency stated that Complainant used all her annual and sick leave from December 20, 2019 through February 6, 2020; she was subsequently granted LWOP on February 7 – 29, 2020 (80 hours), March 2 – 26, 2020 (480 hours), and March 26 – August 7, 2020 (421 hours). Complainant indicated that she was in an approved LWOP status from March 4, 2020, through August 10, 2020. Complainant remained in AWOL since August 10, 2020. The AJ found no discrimination as Complainant alleged. Specifically, the AJ stated that Complainant did not establish that the Agency failed to provide her with a reasonable accommodation in that she failed to provide medical documentation the Agency requested showing that she was able to perform her position duty, i.e., examining patients physically. The AJ found: Complainant alleges only that she suffered from her inability to use her right arm. She has provided limited documentation to support having any disability, and all the documentation provided stated the treating physician would reassess in weeks to come. Despite repeated requests, Complainant failed to offer any medical documentation of a diagnosis of her condition, or a duration; i.e. whether it was temporary or permanent. She failed to sign a release authorizing the Agency to obtain medical information; and she failed to offer a release authorizing medical information to be disclosed even to the investigator in this case. The AJ further found: Complainant has not shown that she would be able to work from home as, by her own admission, she was unable to use a pen or computer on her own. Additionally, the permanent accommodation requested, telework, is one that Complainant is not qualified for as telework would require an increase in use of the computer. Further, as, part of her responsibilities as a [Primary Care Physician], Complainant is required to examine patients physically even as a telework clinician. Complainant stated she was unable to do so on March 4, 2020[,] and after that never provided any documentation that she was able to examine patients. Complainant refused to engage with the Agency on discussions regarding this issue by failing to provide medical documentation, therefore causing the Agency to close her case without a denial or approval. The Agency did not issue a final order and the AJ’s decision effectively became its final action. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i). Complainant appeals from the Agency’s final order, contesting its finding of no discrimination. On appeal, Complainant submits numerous documents, including subsequent doctors’ statements.
items.record:
# FINDINGS

## Factual Background

Complainant was employed as a GS-15 Primary Care Physician at the Agency's East Orange Veterans Affairs Medical Center, beginning March 3, 2019, subject to a two-year probationary period. Her essential duties included conducting daily patient interviews and examinations (typically 12 patients), documenting visits in the electronic medical record system, and ordering consults, labs, and medications.

Complainant sustained an initial shoulder injury on July 12, 2019, which she did not report to supervisors at that time. In December 2019, she aggravated a prior right shoulder injury and notified supervisors shortly thereafter. She claimed this condition prevented her from lifting her right arm, using a mouse or keyboard, writing, performing physical examinations, documenting notes, or using a computer for extended periods.

## Claim 1: Denial of Reasonable Accommodation

**Request and Initial Processing**

Complainant's supervisor became aware of her shoulder condition in December 2019. On February 25, 2020, Complainant made a verbal reasonable accommodation request, requesting no lifting, no prolonged upper extremity fine manipulation, part-time (20 hours per week) light duties, no grabbing, and assistance with computer tasks. Complainant returned to work on March 2, 2020, under the approved restriction of four hours per day with four hours Leave Without Pay (LWOP), five days per week. She was required to complete online training modules and see two to three patients by week's end.

Complainant failed to complete either requirement. On March 4, 2020, she declined to see a waiting patient, citing shoulder pain and inability to write notes.

**Interactive Process**

On March 5, 2020, the supervisor, second-level supervisor, and Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator initiated an interactive process. During this meeting, Complainant stated she could not perform patient examinations, complete patient paperwork, or use a computer for more than a few minutes. The Agency decided to grant LWOP for six weeks to allow injury rehabilitation.

Two weeks later, Complainant requested 100% telework. The Agency took the following steps to accommodate her:

- Prepared dictation software for installation
- Ordered two ergonomic chairs for exam rooms
- Shipped ergonomic mouse and keyboard to her home with duplicates for the office
- Approved a laptop on March 3, 2020 (delivery delayed due to equipment shortage)
- Submitted a second laptop request through the Computer/Electronic Accommodation (CAP) program, which was denied because Complainant failed to provide sufficient medical documentation during the needs assessment
- Secured a laptop for Complainant by June 2, 2020

The Agency offered telework for one to three months, contingent upon medical documentation justifying the need. This offer required Complainant to sign a telework agreement; Complainant refused.

**Medical Documentation Requests**

On April 21, 2020, Complainant made another accommodation request for 100% telework, 20 hours per week, and modified work assignments (one year to permanent). The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator made numerous requests—including several emails in June 2020—for medical documentation of Complainant's disability and requested information regarding:

- The effectiveness of telework/telemedicine accommodation relative to her medical condition
- The duration of her medical condition
- Consent to contact her physician

Complainant failed to provide such documentation.

**Medical Records Provided**

The record reflects Complainant provided the following medical documentation:

- **DR1 (January 13, 2020)**: Clearance to return to work after February 10, 2020 follow-up
- **DR1 (February 10, 2020)**: Clearance to return to work on March 2, 2020
- **DR2 (February 25, 2020)**: Light duty, part-time work, no lifting, computer assistance needed; six-week reevaluation
- **DR2 (April 21, 2020)**: Light duty, work from home via laptop and telemedicine; reevaluation on May 19, 2020
- **DR2 (May 19, 2020)**: Two statements indicating dexterity issues, continued physical therapy, ability to use computer with ergonomic support; six-week reevaluation
- **DR2 (June 22, 2020, submitted July 15)**: Maximum 20 hours weekly telework, pain, dexterity and gripping issues, continued physical therapy, ability to use computer with ergonomic support; six-week reevaluation
- **DR2 (July 30, 2020)**: Reiterated previous statement, recommended back specialist evaluation, shoulder symptoms "well controlled," and patient "discharged"

**Closure of Accommodation Request**

On August 7, 2020, the Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator closed Complainant's reasonable accommodation request, informing her the case would reopen if requested documentation was provided.

## Claim 2: AWOL Charge

After Complainant's reasonable accommodation case was closed, the Coordinator suggested it was reasonable to charge Complainant with Absent Without Leave. Management decided to place her in AWOL status beginning August 10, 2020. The record reflects Complainant had not worked for nearly eight months.

The Agency documented that Complainant:
- Used all annual and sick leave from December 20, 2019 through February 6, 2020
- Received LWOP: February 7-29, 2020 (80 hours); March 2-26, 2020 (480 hours); and March 26-August 7, 2020 (421 hours)

Complainant remained in AWOL status from August 10, 2020 through her termination on January 22, 2021.

## Administrative Judge's Decision

The Administrative Judge found no discrimination. The AJ determined that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency denied reasonable accommodation because she failed to provide medical documentation demonstrating her ability to perform essential position duties, specifically physical patient examinations.

The AJ noted:

- Complainant provided limited disability documentation; all documentation indicated reassessments would occur within weeks
- Despite repeated requests, Complainant failed to provide medical diagnosis, condition duration, or whether the condition was temporary or permanent
- Complainant failed to sign a release authorizing the Agency to obtain medical information or authorize disclosure to the investigator
- By Complainant's own admission on March 4, 2020, she could not use a pen or computer independently
- Telework, the permanent accommodation requested, would require increased computer use, contrary to her stated limitations
- As a Primary Care Physician, Complainant must perform physical patient examinations, even as a telework clinician, which she stated she was unable to do on March 4, 2020, and never subsequently provided documentation showing capability
- Complainant refused to engage with the Agency by failing to provide requested medical documentation, causing closure of her accommodation case without approval or denial

In response, on March 25, 2020, S1 requested Complainant provide physician documentation regarding her ability to perform essential functions of her position including her limitations with typing notes, placing orders including consults, sending out lab letters, and filling out paperwork and forms as requested by her patients. During this time period, due to COVID-19, non-urgent appointments were cancelled, and telework arrangements were made for hospital physicians on ad hoc basis, i.e., 50% telework alternating weeks in-person in the hospital and at-home teleworking. Meanwhile, the Agency prepared dictation software to be installed in Complainant’s computer (to minimize typing); two ergonomic chairs to be delivered to her office for each of her exam rooms; and an ergonomic mouse and keyboard were shipped to her home and a second set was delivered to her office. A laptop was approved on March 3, 2020, but the delivery was delayed due to a shortage of equipment. S1 sent a second laptop request through the Computer/Electronic Accommodation program (CAP), within the Department of Defense, to try to get one sooner but the CAP denied the request because during the “Needs Assessment,” Complainant failed to submit sufficient medical documentation to support the need for a second laptop, as well as a telework agreement. On June 2, 2020, the Agency secured a laptop for Complainant, but she never signed a telework agreement, i.e., addressing teleworking for one to three months due to her temporary disability. S1 indicated that the Agency could not offer Complainant’s requested unconditional 100% telework for at least a year because she failed to provide medical documentation to justify the request. Further, S1 stated that the hospital had a shortage of physicians, some providers were sick with COVID-19, and Complainant’s patients were being covered by other physicians. Thus, the Agency decided to offer Complainant a telework agreement for one to three months, dependent upon updates to her medical documentation. Complainant did not accept the Agency’s telework agreement. The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator indicated that Complainant made several accommodation requests, including one on April 21, 2020. Complainant requested 100% telework, 20 hours per work week, and modified work assignments for one year to permanent basis. The Coordinator stated, and the record reflects, that she made numerous requests, including several emails in June 2020, to Complainant for medical documentation of her disability in connection with her reasonable accommodation requests. Complainant failed to provide such documentation. Specifically, the Coordinator stated that Complainant was asked to provide medical documentations relating to the effectiveness of telework/telemedicine accommodation with her medical condition and the information relating to the duration of her medical condition, including her consent to contact her physician in order to proceed with her accommodation request. Complainant failed to provide such information. Thus, on August 7, 2020, the Coordinator closed Complainant’s request for reasonable accommodation and informed her that the case would be reopened if she provided the requested documentation. The record reflects that Complainant provided the Agency a copy of her doctor’s (DR1) Return to Work statements. In a Return to Work, dated January 13, 2020, DR1 indicated that Complainant was seen in his office on January 13, 2020, and may return to work after follow-up on February 10, 2020. In a Return to Work, dated February 10, 2020, DR1 indicated that Complainant was seen in his office on February 10, 2020, and may return to work on March 2, 2020. The record also reflects that Complainant provided a doctor’s (DR2) statement dated February 25, 2020. Therein, DR2 stated that Complainant was under DR2’s care for her right shoulder; she should be given light duty and part-time work with no lifting; she should be given assistance with computer tasks; and her return to full duty would be reevaluated in six weeks. In DR2’s statement, dated April 21, 2020, DR2 indicated that Complainant should be allowed to continue in light duty, work from home via laptop, and telemedicine; and her status to return to full duty would be reevaluated on May 19, 2020. In two statements, both dated May 19, 2020, DR2 stated that Complainant was evaluated on May 19, 2020, for right shoulder; she had dexterity issues; she was to continue in physical therapy to oversee shoulder exercises and working from home via telemedicine; she was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support; and her status to return to normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks. The record indicates that on July 15, 2020, Complainant submitted DR2’s statement dated June 22, 2020. Therein, DR2 stated that Complainant should be allowed to work from home via telemedicine, maximum 20 hours weekly; she was in pain with dexterity issues; she had issues with gripping and right arm/hand manipulation; she reported pain and issues with gripping the wheel when driving; she would continue with physical therapy to oversee shoulder exercises; she was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support; and her status to resume normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks. In a statement dated July 30, 2020, DR2, reiterating the foregoing statement, indicated that he was recommending an evaluation with a back specialist for Complainant’s condition; her status to return would be reevaluated; and her “shoulder symptoms are well controlled and is discharged at this time.” Regarding claim 2, S1 and S2 indicated that after Complainant’s reasonable accommodation case was closed, the Coordinator suggested it was reasonable to charge Complainant AWOL for her absence. Considering the Coordinator’s suggestion and the fact that Complainant had not worked for nearly eight months without providing medical documentation as requested, management decided to place her in AWOL starting August 10, 2020. The Agency stated that Complainant used all her annual and sick leave from December 20, 2019 through February 6, 2020; she was subsequently granted LWOP on February 7 – 29, 2020 (80 hours), March 2 – 26, 2020 (480 hours), and March 26 – August 7, 2020 (421 hours). Complainant indicated that she was in an approved LWOP status from March 4, 2020, through August 10, 2020. Complainant remained in AWOL since August 10, 2020. The AJ found no discrimination as Complainant alleged. Specifically, the AJ stated that Complainant did not establish that the Agency failed to provide her with a reasonable accommodation in that she failed to provide medical documentation the Agency requested showing that she was able to perform her position duty, i.e., examining patients physically. The AJ found: Complainant alleges only that she suffered from her inability to use her right arm. She has provided limited documentation to support having any disability, and all the documentation provided stated the treating physician would reassess in weeks to come. Despite repeated requests, Complainant failed to offer any medical documentation of a diagnosis of her condition, or a duration; i.e. whether it was temporary or permanent. She failed to sign a release authorizing the Agency to obtain medical information; and she failed to offer a release authorizing medical information to be disclosed even to the investigator in this case. The AJ further found: Complainant has not shown that she would be able to work from home as, by her own admission, she was unable to use a pen or computer on her own. Additionally, the permanent accommodation requested, telework, is one that Complainant is not qualified for as telework would require an increase in use of the computer. Further, as, part of her responsibilities as a [Primary Care Physician], Complainant is required to examine patients physically even as a telework clinician. Complainant stated she was unable to do so on March 4, 2020[,] and after that never provided any documentation that she was able to examine patients. Complainant refused to engage with the Agency on discussions regarding this issue by failing to provide medical documentation, therefore causing the Agency to close her case without a denial or approval. The Agency did not issue a final order and the AJ’s decision effectively became its final action. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i). Complainant appeals from the Agency’s final order, contesting its finding of no discrimination. On appeal, Complainant submits numerous documents, including subsequent doctors’ statements.

# FINDINGS

## Factual Background

Complainant was employed as a GS-15 Primary Care Physician at the Agency's East Orange Veterans Affairs Medical Center, beginning March 3, 2019, subject to a two-year probationary period. Her essential duties included conducting daily patient interviews and examinations (typically 12 patients), documenting visits in the electronic medical record system, and ordering consults, labs, and medications.

Complainant sustained an initial shoulder injury on July 12, 2019, which she did not report to supervisors at that time. In December 2019, she aggravated a prior right shoulder injury and notified supervisors shortly thereafter. She claimed this condition prevented her from lifting her right arm, using a mouse or keyboard, writing, performing physical examinations, documenting notes, or using a computer for extended periods.

## Claim 1: Denial of Reasonable Accommodation

**Request and Initial Processing**

Complainant's supervisor became aware of her shoulder condition in December 2019. On February 25, 4020, Complainant made a verbal reasonable accommodation request, requesting no lifting, no prolonged upper extremity fine manipulation, part-time (20 hours per week) light duties, no grabbing, and assistance with computer tasks. Complainant returned to work on March 2, 2020, under the approved restriction of four hours per day with four hours Leave Without Pay (LWOP), five days per week. She was required to complete online training modules and see two to three patients by week's end.

Complainant failed to complete either requirement. On March 4, 2020, she declined to see a waiting patient, citing shoulder pain and inability to write notes.

**Interactive Process**

On March 5, 2020, the supervisor, second-level supervisor, and Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator initiated an interactive process. During this meeting, Complainant stated she could not perform patient examinations, complete patient paperwork, or use a computer for more than a few minutes. The Agency decided to grant LWOP for six weeks to allow injury rehabilitation.

Two weeks later, Complainant requested 100% telework. The Agency took the following steps to accommodate her:

- Prepared dictation software for installation
- Ordered two ergonomic chairs for exam rooms
- Shipped ergonomic mouse and keyboard to her home with duplicates for the office
- Approved a laptop on March 3, 2020 (delivery delayed due to equipment shortage)
- Submitted a second laptop request through the Computer/Electronic Accommodation (CAP) program, which was denied because Complainant failed to provide sufficient medical documentation during the needs assessment
- Secured a laptop for Complainant by June 2, 2020

The Agency offered telework for one to three months, contingent upon medical documentation justifying the need. This offer required Complainant to sign a telework agreement; Complainant refused.

**Medical Documentation Requests**

On April 21, 2020, Complainant made another accommodation request for 100% telework, 20 hours per week, and modified work assignments (one year to permanent). The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator made numerous requests—including several emails in June 2020—for medical documentation of Complainant's disability and requested information regarding:

- The effectiveness of telework/telemedicine accommodation relative to her medical condition
- The duration of her medical condition
- Consent to contact her physician

Complainant failed to provide such documentation.

**Medical Records Provided**

The record reflects Complainant provided the following medical documentation:

- **DR1 (January 13, 2020)**: Clearance to return to work after February 10, 2020 follow-up
- **DR1 (February 10, 2020)**: Clearance to return to work on March 2, 2020
- **DR2 (February 25, 2020)**: Light duty, part-time work, no lifting, computer assistance needed; six-week reevaluation
- **DR2 (April 21, 2020)**: Light duty, work from home via laptop and telemedicine; reevaluation on May 19, 2020
- **DR2 (May 19, 2020)**: Two statements indicating dexterity issues, continued physical therapy, ability to use computer with ergonomic support; six-week reevaluation
- **DR2 (June 22, 2020, submitted July 15)**: Maximum 20 hours weekly telework, pain, dexterity and gripping issues, continued physical therapy, ability to use computer with ergonomic support; six-week reevaluation
- **DR2 (July 30, 2020)**: Reiterated previous statement, recommended back specialist evaluation, shoulder symptoms "well controlled," and patient "discharged"

**Closure of Accommodation Request**

On August 7, 2020, the Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator closed Complainant's reasonable accommodation request, informing her the case would reopen if requested documentation was provided.

## Claim 2: AWOL Charge

After Complainant's reasonable accommodation case was closed, the Coordinator suggested it was reasonable to charge Complainant with Absent Without Leave. Management decided to place her in AWOL status beginning August 10, 2020. The record reflects Complainant had not worked for nearly eight months.

The Agency documented that Complainant:
- Used all annual and sick leave from December 20, 2019 through February 6, 2020
- Received LWOP: February 7-29, 2020 (80 hours); March 2-26, 2020 (480 hours); and March 26-August 7, 2020 (421 hours)

Complainant remained in AWOL status from August 10, 2020 through her termination on January 22, 2021.

## Administrative Judge's Decision

The Administrative Judge found no discrimination. The AJ determined that Complainant failed to establish that the Agency denied reasonable accommodation because she failed to provide medical documentation demonstrating her ability to perform essential position duties, specifically physical patient examinations.

The AJ noted:

- Complainant provided limited disability documentation; all documentation indicated reassessments would occur within weeks
- Despite repeated requests, Complainant failed to provide medical diagnosis, condition duration, or whether the condition was temporary or permanent
- Complainant failed to sign a release authorizing the Agency to obtain medical information or authorize disclosure to the investigator
- By Complainant's own admission on March 4, 2020, she could not use a pen or computer independently
- Telework, the permanent accommodation requested, would require increased computer use, contrary to her stated limitations
- As a Primary Care Physician, Complainant must perform physical patient examinations, even as a telework clinician, which she stated she was unable to do on March 4, 2020, and never subsequently provided documentation showing capability
- Complainant refused to engage with the Agency by failing to provide requested medical documentation, causing closure of her accommodation case without approval or denial

In 2015, Section Chief acknowledged she deserved a promotion but delayed processing the paperwork until 2017, during a hiring freeze. She was notified of the hiring freeze in February 2017, and that it was indefinite. 4 c. On May 12, 2017, Section Chief yelled loudly and laughed at her, saying, "no wonder nothing you ever do works" within earshot of colleagues when she answered his question about a protocol. d. In late May or June 2017, Section Chief laughed with another colleague and a new trainee about the time he required her to work on Christmas day. e. Section Chief approached her and pressured her to disclose her political affiliation. f. In late December 2013 or 2014, Section Chief expressed to her his surprise that she wrote well. 5 11. On February 23, 2018, Section Chief failed to promote her. 12. In March 2018, Lab Chief re-positioned her photograph under a different lab group in the breakroom, although she was still a member of the Section. 14. On March 14, 2018, Section Chief did not communicate with her about an ongoing collaborative project, and because Section Chief did not speak directly to RMO-2 about the project, Complainant was unable to work on it. The Agency’s definition of this incident did not include the month in 2017. But Complainant stated she recalled two incidents, and the second was in April 2017. Report of Investigation (ROI), Ex. F-1 (Complainant’s affidavit) Bates No. 123. The Agency’s definition of this incident did not include the month in 2017. # FINDINGS SECTION

## Background and Legal Standards

The Complainant, an African American female biologist of Guyanese national origin employed at the Agency's National Institute on Aging, filed an EEO complaint on November 8, 2017, alleging discrimination and reprisal based on race/color, national origin, sex, disability, and prior protected EEO activity. The complaint, as amended, contained 17 numbered allegations spanning the period from 2009 through April 2018.

The Administrative Judge (AJ) dismissed allegations 6 through 11 as untimely under the 300-day statute of limitations for initiating EEO counseling (or the extended 45-day period in jurisdictions with deferral agreements). The Agency subsequently investigated the remaining allegations and issued a decision finding no discrimination on any of the claims.

On appeal, the Complainant raises a procedural challenge regarding the inordinate delay in issuing the Final Agency Decision (FAD), arguing that more than 15 months elapsed following the AJ's 60-day remand period, warranting a default judgment as a sanction.

## Findings on Procedural Timeliness

**Finding 1: Failure to Issue Timely Final Agency Decision**

The record demonstrates that the Agency failed to comply with the mandatory timeline for issuing a Final Agency Decision following the AJ's remand. The 60-day period established by regulation expired without the issuance of a FAD. The Complainant's documentation shows that on May 20, 2020, she was compelled to inquire about the status of the FAD, indicating a delay of more than 15 months from the time the AJ's remand should have prompted Agency action. This extraordinary tardiness constitutes a procedural violation.

**Finding 2: Lack of Agency Response to Appeal**

The record reflects that the Agency did not file a response to the Complainant's appeal regarding the untimely FAD. This failure to respond compounds the procedural deficiency and prevents the presentation of any justification or explanation for the substantial delay.

## Findings on Substantive Allegations

The Agency's investigation and dismissal of Claims 6 through 11 as untimely is upheld on grounds of the statute of limitations. These allegations, spanning 2009 through May 2017, were not the subject of EEO counseling within the required timeframe.

Regarding the remaining allegations (Claims 1-5, 12-17), the Agency found no discrimination. However, given the extraordinary procedural delays and the Agency's failure to respond to the appeal, these findings are subject to review based on the potential prejudice to the Complainant caused by the procedural violations.

## Conclusion Regarding Appropriate Remedy

The manifest procedural failure to timely issue a Final Agency Decision, combined with the Agency's failure to respond to the Complainant's good-faith appeal, raises serious concerns regarding the integrity of the administrative process and the Complainant's right to a timely adjudication.

**Finding 2: Lack of Agency Response to Appeal**

The record reflects that the Agency did not file a response to the Complainant's appeal regarding the untimely FAD. This failure to respond compounds the procedural deficiency and prevents the presentation of any justification or explanation for the substantial delay.

## Findings on Substantive Allegations

The Agency's investigation and dismissal of Claims 6 through 11 as untimely is upheld on grounds of the statute of limitations. These allegations, spanning 2009 through May 2017, were not the subject of EEO counseling within the required timeframe.

Regarding the remaining allegations (Claims 1-5, 12-17), the Agency found no discrimination. However, given the extraordinary procedural delays and the Agency's failure to respond to the appeal, these findings are subject to review based on the potential prejudice to the Complainant caused by the procedural violations.

## Conclusion Regarding Appropriate Remedy

The manifest procedural failure to timely issue a Final Agency Decision, combined with the Agency's failure to respond to the Complainant's good-faith appeal, raises serious concerns regarding the integrity of the administrative process and the Complainant's right to a timely adjudication.

# FINDINGS

## Background and Allegations

At the time of the events at issue, Complainant was employed as a probationary Credentials Assistant, GS-0303-07, at the Agency's Naval Medical Center in Portsmouth, Virginia. On November 8, 2018, Complainant filed an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on race (African-American) when she was terminated from her probationary position on August 2, 2018. Following the investigation, an EEO Administrative Judge (AJ) held a hearing and issued a decision in favor of the Agency.

## Theory of Discrimination

Complainant's primary theory of discrimination, presented at the hearing, alleged that her second-level supervisor (S2), Department Head, GS-0301-12, terminated her after learning that Complainant's significant other was White. Complainant testified that S2 became aware of this relationship in May 2018 and that her working relationship with S2 deteriorated thereafter. Complainant further testified that her first-level supervisor (S1), Professional Affairs Coordinator, GS-0301-11, had warned her not to disclose the interracial relationship to S2.

Complainant presented a coworker (CW), Program Analyst, GS-0303-07, as a corroborating witness. CW testified that S2 made openly discriminatory statements regarding interracial relationships and expressed surprise at Complainant's dating a White man. Both Complainant and CW testified that S1 had warned them about S2's alleged prejudice.

## Credibility Findings

The AJ found the testimony regarding the interracial relationship theory to be lacking in credibility. The AJ noted that this theory was conspicuously absent from: (1) Complainant's initial EEO complaint; (2) the EEO counseling records; and (3) Complainant's affidavit submitted during the investigation phase. The AJ determined that such evidence, if credible, would not logically have surfaced for the first time approximately three years after the termination.

During the earlier phases of the investigation, Complainant had articulated different theories for her termination, neither of which related to her race. Specifically, Complainant had attributed her termination to: (1) events that occurred during a work conference in Leesburg, Virginia, where S2 allegedly engaged in inappropriate behavior and subsequently distrusted Complainant; and (2) S2's mistaken belief that Complainant had filed a grievance against her (when it was actually another employee).

The AJ similarly found credibility deficiencies in CW's testimony. CW's affidavit submitted during the investigation made no reference to Complainant's interracial relationship or S2's opposition to such relationships. Instead, CW's affidavit attributed the alleged discrimination to Complainant being "an African-American with more experience than management." When cross-examined, Complainant was unable to provide any explanation for her failure to raise the interracial relationship theory prior to the hearing.

The AJ also found S1 to be not credible when S1 testified at the hearing. S1 denied making any comments characterizing S2 as racist, contradicting the testimony of Complainant and CW.

## Legitimate, Nondiscriminatory Reason for Termination

The AJ found that the Agency articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for Complainant's termination as set forth in the Notice of Termination. The stated reason was Complainant's failure to "follow the privileging/credentialing process when [she] misrepresented to [her] leadership that a provider had specifically requested privileges when in fact [Complainant] made the request."

The underlying facts demonstrated that Complainant had provided inaccurate guidance to a healthcare provider regarding the credentialing process. The provider relied on Complainant's mistaken instructions when submitting his application, resulting in his selection of incorrect privileges. Complainant's acknowledged inaccurate guidance delayed the provider's application and prevented timely credential approval until the provider's existing privileges were set to expire.

When the provider subsequently contacted Complainant's supervisors to express frustration with the delay, Complainant provided an explanation to S1 that was inconsistent with the facts as later determined. S2 obtained a written statement from the provider and concluded that Complainant had misrepresented the circumstances, forming part of the basis for her termination.

At the hearing, the provider was called as a witness and was found credible when he testified that he and Complainant had discussed the application prior to his submission and that he had relied on her instructions. The AJ found Complainant "not credible in her testimony that she never spoke to [the provider] prior to him submitting the [first] application."

## Pretext Analysis

The AJ concluded that Complainant failed to establish pretext because no evidence demonstrated that a similarly situated employee identified by Complainant was involved in a similar credentialing error or had engaged in similar dishonesty with management.

However, the AJ identified a secondary basis for termination cited in the Notice of Termination—that Complainant "failed to initiate the renewal privileging/credentialing process within 90 days as required." The AJ found that this allegation was factually untrue and that a similarly situated employee had multiple renewals nearing expiration with less than 90 days remaining but was not terminated. The AJ noted that had this been the sole stated reason for termination, Complainant might have demonstrated pretext. However, the AJ concluded that the primary reason—Complainant's misrepresentation regarding the provider's requested privileges—was the dispositive basis for the termination and was supported by substantial evidence.

## Credibility and Candor Issues

The AJ emphasized that Complainant's lack of credibility was particularly significant given that her "lack of candor was part of why she was terminated." The AJ found Complainant's testimony "simply unreliable" and noted that her credibility was "doubly important in this case."

## Final Agency Action

The Agency failed to issue a final order within forty days of receipt of the AJ's decision. Pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i), the AJ's decision finding that Complainant failed to prove discrimination became the Agency's final action.

## Conclusion

Based on the AJ's findings, the Agency did not discriminate against Complainant based on race in the termination of her probationary employment. The termination was supported by a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason—Complainant's misrepresentation regarding the credentialing process—which Complainant failed to rebut with credible evidence of pretext.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Travel Specialist, GS-6, at the Agency’s Office of Infectious Disease (OID), National Center for HIV/AIDS, Viral Hepatitis, STD and TB Prevention (NCHHSTP) in Atlanta, Georgia. Report of Investigation (ROI), at 49. 2 The Supervisor Program Specialist, GS-12, (female, African American) was assigned as Complainant’s first-level supervisor (S1). Complainant was also supervised by the Management Officer (male, Caucasian) and the Deputy Director (male). Page numbers refer to the Bates page numbers appearing at the bottom center of each page of the ROI. According to Complainant, on October 28, 2013, in a meeting, S1 told her to get out of the Agency because upper management did not like her, the Management Officer was out to get her, and that she needed to get out of the “god damn” Union because it was never going to allow her to go anywhere in her career. ROI at 127. S1 denied making the comments and denied that the meeting or incident ever took place. Also, according to Complainant, the Support Specialist asked why she was not attending the Christmas party and asked if she celebrated Christmas. Id. at 129-30. Complainant apparently replied that she is a Jehovah’s Witness and does not celebrate Christmas. Id. Complainant averred that the Support Specialist “looked at her as if she had a disease” and rolled her eyes. Id. The Support Specialist did not recall having any interaction with Complainant on the day in question and maintained that the incident did not occur as Complainant alleged. Complainant additionally averred that on January 9, 2014, she overheard a coworker (C1) make the comment to another coworker (C2) that she (Complainant) thinks “she is cute because she is built like a Black girl" and that she (Complainant) "is bad news and not your friend." Id. at 131- 32. Complainant maintained that such comments were made about her multiple times in hallways and in the elevator. Id. But C1 maintained that she had no idea who Complainant was and that she did not make any such comment. C2 similarly averred that she did not recall the comment being made to her by C1. Complainant further attested that the Deputy Director sexually harassed her on multiple occasions, which continued to the present. Complainant stated that the Deputy Director would stare at her chest, and he also put his hand on her left leg and “rolled his hand down” during two separate staff meetings. Id. at 133-35. Complainant said that she simply “scooted over” when the Deputy Director first put his hand on her leg. Id. She said that when this occurred a second time, she left in the middle of the meeting. Id. Complainant added that she told the Deputy Director to stop because the touching of her leg during the meeting was making her feel uncomfortable. Id. Complainant averred that the Deputy Director would also often come into her cubicle and put his hands on her shoulders, as if he were massaging her. Id. Complainant further stated that the Deputy Director would lean over her while showing her something on her computer, invading her personal space. Id. Complainant stated that the Deputy Director also asked her to lunch and/or dinner, but she rebuffed his advances. Id. Complainant attested that the Deputy Director punished her for rebuffing him by assigning her extra duties, refusing her requests for training, assigning her duties outside of her position description, and yelling and cursing at her in his office regarding the processing of employees travel preparations. Id. at 53. Complainant also attested that the Deputy Director would often call her into his office and “vent in a loud, angry voice while throwing things such as pens and pencils across the room.” Id. at 154. Complainant explained that she discussed the Deputy Director’s behavior with several of her coworkers. Complainant further explained that she reported the Deputy Director’s behavior just a few weeks after it first occurred to the Director, who simply shook his head in disbelief. Id. at 134. Complainant maintained that nothing was done to resolve the situation, and so the harassment continued. Id. Complainant stated that she further reported the Deputy Director’s harassment to S1, the Management Officer, and a Consultant with the Agency. Id. According to Complainant, these management officials ignored her complaints about the Deputy Director’s harassment towards her. Id. Nevertheless, both S1 and the Management Officer denied that Complainant ever reported the Deputy Director’s behavior to them, and so they were unaware of the Deputy Director’s alleged harassment. However, several of Complainant’s coworkers averred that Complainant had confided in them that the Deputy Director had been subjecting her to sexual harassment. The Senior Budget Analyst specifically attested that Complainant would come into her office, almost on a weekly basis, to vent about the Deputy Director violating her personal space and making her feel uncomfortable by asking her out and making inappropriate comments. Id. at 208. The Senior Budget Analyst said that she had witnessed the Deputy Director throw tantrums and yell as if Complainant was his “soundboard” on a few occasions. Id. The Senior Budget Analyst further averred that Complainant visited her office on several occasions crying over the Deputy Director’s behavior towards her. Id. The Team Lead similarly attested that Complainant also came to him on occasions to talk about the Deputy Director’s inappropriate behavior and that the Deputy Director had touched her inappropriately during a meeting. Id. at 205. The Team Lead averred that Complainant explained to him that she had scheduled a meeting with the Management Officer to discuss the Deputy Director’s conduct, and that Complainant later discussed the Management Officer’s lack of concern for addressing the alleged harassment. Id. The Team Lead added that he told Complainant that it seemed as if nothing would come as a result of her meeting with the Management Officer. Id. The Resource Management Team Lead also explained that she was frequently a “comforting ear” for Complainant, and that Complainant expressed her extreme discomfort with the Deputy Director’s behavior. Id. at 223. The Resource Management Team Lead stated that she had seen the Deputy Director in Complainant’s office many times, but she had not witnessed anything more than what she perceived to be an encroachment of Complainant’s personal space. Id. She mentioned she felt this to be unusual, but she had never directly witnessed the Deputy Director touch or address Complainant inappropriately. Id. The Public Health Advisor Supervisor likewise maintained that Complainant had mentioned that the Deputy Director had touched her leg and asked her out to dinner. Id. at 199. The Public Health Advisor attested that the Deputy Director had harassed her in the past as well, but she did not complain because she would have been the first women to have come forward. Id. The Public Health Advisor said that she was afraid to come forward because the Deputy Director was highly regarded within the Agency. Id. Another Team Lead, and two more employees, similarly stated that Complainant had mentioned that the Deputy Director had been harassing her. Complainant claimed, moreover, that S1 improperly scored her with the unsatisfactory rating of 2. for her mid-year performance review and placed her on a Performance Assistance Plan (PAP). # FINDINGS

## Overview

This investigation examined eleven allegations of discrimination and harassment filed by the Complainant, a Travel Specialist, GS-6, at the Agency's Office of Infectious Disease (OID), National Center for HIV/AIDS, Viral Hepatitis, STD and TB Prevention (NCHHSTP) in Atlanta, Georgia. The Complainant alleged discrimination and harassment based on race (Caucasian), national origin (German, Persian), sex (female), religion (Jehovah's Witness, Jewish), and reprisal for protected EEO activity occurring between October 2013 and January 2015.

## Findings on Substantive Allegations

### Claims 1, 2, 3, and 5 – Alleged Hostile Work Environment

The investigation examined four separate allegations regarding statements and conduct allegedly directed at the Complainant by her first-level supervisor (S1), a Business Services Support Specialist, and a coworker.

**Claim 1 (October 28, 2013):** The Complainant alleged that S1 told her to leave the Agency, stated that upper management did not like her, claimed the Management Officer was "out to get her," and told her to leave the Union. S1 denied making these comments and denied that the meeting occurred. No corroborating evidence was found to support the Complainant's version of events. The Agency concluded that the Complainant failed to establish this allegation.

**Claim 2 (December 12, 2013):** The Complainant alleged that the Business Services Support Specialist questioned why she did not attend the Christmas party and asked if she celebrated Christmas. When the Complainant indicated she was a Jehovah's Witness and did not celebrate Christmas, the Specialist allegedly looked at her "as if she had a disease" and rolled her eyes. The Support Specialist did not recall this interaction and maintained the alleged incident did not occur. The Agency concluded that insufficient evidence corroborated the Complainant's allegations.

**Claim 3 (January 9, 2014):** The Complainant alleged that she overheard coworkers (C1 and C2) making derogatory comments about her, stating she "thinks she is cute because she is built like a Black girl" and is "bad news and not your friend." The Complainant asserted these comments were made repeatedly in hallways and elevators. C1 denied knowing the Complainant and denied making the alleged comment. C2 did not recall the comment being made. The Agency found insufficient corroboration for the Complainant's version of events.

**Claim 5 (January 13, 2014):** The Complainant alleged that S1 told her to "get the hell out of my office" when she attempted to discuss training concerns. S1 denied this incident occurred, and no corroborating evidence was located. The Agency concluded the Complainant failed to establish this allegation.

**Conclusion on Claims 1-3 and 5:** The Agency determined that the Complainant failed to prove these allegations occurred as alleged. The investigation found no evidence to corroborate the Complainant's version of events regarding S1's alleged hostile conduct. Furthermore, even if the allegations had been substantiated, the Agency determined they were not severe or pervasive enough to constitute a hostile work environment sufficient to support a discrimination claim.

### Claim 4 – Sexual Harassment by Deputy Director

The Complainant alleged that the Deputy Director sexually harassed her from 2006 onward, including unwanted physical contact (touching her leg and rolling his hand down her leg during staff meetings, placing hands on her shoulders as if massaging her), invading her personal space while leaning over her at her computer, and making unwanted social invitations to lunch and/or dinner. The Complainant further alleged that she was punished for rejecting his advances through assignment of extra duties, denial of training requests, duties outside her position description, and verbal abuse including yelling and cursing.

**Supporting Evidence:** Multiple coworkers provided evidence that the Complainant had confided in them about the Deputy Director's conduct:
- The Senior Budget Analyst testified that the Complainant visited nearly weekly to vent about the Deputy Director violating her personal space, making inappropriate comments, and asking her out. The Senior Budget Analyst witnessed the Deputy Director's angry outbursts and observed the Complainant visiting her office crying.
- The Team Lead testified that the Complainant reported inappropriate physical contact during a meeting and discussed her lack of success in addressing the matter with the Management Officer.
- The Resource Management Team Lead described observing the Deputy Director frequently in the Complainant's office and noted unusual encroachment of her personal space.
- The Public Health Advisor Supervisor confirmed that the Complainant reported the Deputy Director had touched her leg and asked her out to dinner. This witness also disclosed that she herself had been harassed by the Deputy Director but had not come forward due to fear and the Deputy Director's high regard within the Agency.
- Additional team leads and employees corroborated that the Complainant reported harassment by the Deputy Director.

**Agency's Conclusion:** Despite the consistent reports from multiple witnesses that the Complainant had disclosed being devastated by and frequently venting about the Deputy Director's harassing conduct, the Agency determined that the Complainant failed to establish that she was subjected to sexual harassment. The Agency noted that while witnesses described the Deputy Director as becoming angry and throwing objects, and while witnesses confirmed the Complainant's distress regarding his conduct, no witnesses directly observed the alleged sexual harassment. The Agency concluded there was insufficient evidence to establish that the Deputy Director sexually harassed the Complainant.

### Claims 6-11 – Performance Management Actions

The Complainant alleged discriminatory motivation behind a series of performance management actions: an unsatisfactory mid-year performance review (Claim 6), placement on a Performance Assistance Plan (Claim 7), placement on a Performance Improvement Plan (Claim 8), issuance of a Counseling Memorandum (Claim 9), a supervisor transfer (Claim 10), and an unsatisfactory year-end performance evaluation (Claim 11).

**S1's Performance Management Documentation:** 
- The PAP, dated May 4, 2014, cited specific performance deficiencies including untimely responses to customers regarding travel tickets and failure to ensure accuracy and completeness of travel reports.
- The PIP, dated September 22, 2014, documented an "Achieved Unsatisfactory Results" rating for Customer Service, citing failure to resolve customer complaints independently, incomplete timely task completion, and inadequate customer communication. The PIP specifically referenced multiple customer complaints and a complaint from the Senior Federal Agency Travel Administrator regarding the Complainant's need for constant assistance in completing tasks.
- The Counseling Memorandum, dated October 16, 2014, documented the Complainant's alleged loud, rude tone, verbal abuse, inability to control her temper during the PIP presentation meeting, and alleged accusations of being retaliated against.

**Noted Context:** The Support Services Specialist observed that the Complainant was under extreme distress during this period, describing an incident in the copy room where the Complainant was shaking and appeared to be in a state requiring possible emergency assistance. The Specialist reported that the Complainant attributed her distress to harassment from S1.

**Supervisor Transfer (Claim 10):** On December 12, 2014, the Complainant was informed of a transfer to another team away from S1's supervision, characterized as an opportunity for "a new start." The Complainant acknowledged that the transfer resulted in a more positive working environment.

**Year-End Performance Evaluation:** Despite the supervisor transfer, the Complainant received an unsatisfactory rating of 2 on her year-end performance evaluation from S1.

**Agency's Conclusion:** The Agency determined that management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its performance management actions. The Agency found that the Complainant failed to establish that these reasons were pretextual and did not demonstrate that the actions were motivated by discriminatory animus based on her protected classes. Therefore, the Agency concluded the Complainant failed to establish disparate treatment.

## Overall Conclusion

The Agency concluded that the Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Specifically, the Agency found that:

1. The Complainant did not establish the occurrence of allegations 1-3 and 5 with sufficient corroborating evidence;
2. Even if substantiated, these allegations were insufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute a hostile work environment;
3. The Complainant failed to establish that she was subjected to sexual harassment by the Deputy Director despite credible evidence of her repeated distress regarding his conduct;
4. Management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for all performance management actions (claims 6-11), which the Complainant did not demonstrate were pretextual.

- The PAP, dated May 4, 2014, cited specific performance deficiencies including untimely responses to customers regarding travel tickets and failure to ensure accuracy and completeness of travel reports.
- The PIP, dated September 22, 2014, documented an "Achieved Unsatisfactory Results" rating for Customer Service, citing failure to resolve customer complaints independently, incomplete timely task completion, and inadequate customer communication. The PIP specifically referenced multiple customer complaints and a complaint from the Senior Federal Agency Travel Administrator regarding the Complainant's need for constant assistance in completing tasks.
- The Counseling Memorandum, dated October 16, 2014, documented the Complainant's alleged loud, rude tone, verbal abuse, inability to control her temper during the PIP presentation meeting, and alleged accusations of being retaliated against.

**Noted Context:** The Support Services Specialist observed that the Complainant was under extreme distress during this period, describing an incident in the copy room where the Complainant was shaking and appeared to be in a state requiring possible emergency assistance. The Specialist reported that the Complainant attributed her distress to harassment from S1.

**Supervisor Transfer (Claim 10):** On December 12, 2014, the Complainant was informed of a transfer to another team away from S1's supervision, characterized as an opportunity for "a new start." The Complainant acknowledged that the transfer resulted in a more positive working environment.

**Year-End Performance Evaluation:** Despite the supervisor transfer, the Complainant received an unsatisfactory rating of 2 on her year-end performance evaluation from S1.

**Agency's Conclusion:** The Agency determined that management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its performance management actions. The Agency found that the Complainant failed to establish that these reasons were pretextual and did not demonstrate that the actions were motivated by discriminatory animus based on her protected classes. Therefore, the Agency concluded the Complainant failed to establish disparate treatment.

## Overall Conclusion

The Agency concluded that the Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Specifically, the Agency found that:

1. The Complainant did not establish the occurrence of allegations 1-3 and 5 with sufficient corroborating evidence;
2. Even if substantiated, these allegations were insufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute a hostile work environment;
3. The Complainant failed to establish that she was subjected to sexual harassment by the Deputy Director despite credible evidence of her repeated distress regarding his conduct;
4. Management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for all performance management actions (claims 6-11), which the Complainant did not demonstrate were pretextual.

# FINDINGS

## Background and Jurisdiction

At the time of the events at issue, the Complainant was employed as a Library Director, NF-1410-IV, at the Agency's Joint Base Andrews facility in Prince George's County, Maryland. The Complainant initially filed a discrimination complaint that included a claim of reprisal for prior EEO activity; however, she withdrew the reprisal claim prior to the hearing before the EEOC Administrative Judge. The case proceeded to an investigation, following which the Agency provided the Complainant with a copy of the investigative report and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Administrative Judge. The Complainant requested a hearing, but the Administrative Judge granted the Agency's motion for summary judgment, finding no genuine issue of material fact to support discrimination claims based on race, sex, color, or age.

## Factual Findings

The record established the following material facts:

1. Between May 31, 2018 and July 16, 2018, the Complainant's first-level supervisor (S1), a Force Development Flight Chief, GS-0301-13, claimed to have provided three verbal counselings to the Complainant; no written documentation was generated or placed in the Complainant's personnel file regarding these counselings.

2. On October 18, 2018, the Complainant received a Letter of Reprimand from S1.

3. Between February 12, 2019 and April 3, 2019, S1 accepted statements from the Complainant's White subordinates regarding the Complainant's conduct without conducting further independent investigation.

4. On April 25, 2019, the Complainant received a Notice of Proposed Removal letter, signed by S1.

5. On or about June 28, 2019, the Complainant was issued a Decision to Remove letter.

6. On October 22, 2019, the Complainant discovered her Common Access Card remained active after her removal from federal service.

## Analysis of Discrimination Claims

### Disparate Treatment and Legitimate Nondiscriminatory Reasons

The Administrative Judge found that, even assuming the Complainant could establish a prima facie case of discrimination regarding the proposed removal and termination (Claims 4 and 5), the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the employment actions. Specifically, S1 documented the following reasons for the removal decision:

- Failure to meet deadlines in a timely manner
- Cancelling scheduled events without permission from leadership
- Failure to stagger schedules to meet patron and event needs
- Failure to relieve staff members for lunches or breaks
- Failure to conduct staff planning meetings for events
- Staff allegations that the Complainant engaged in gossip and disclosed privileged employee information
- Staff concerns regarding potential retaliation, negative feedback, and unfavorable performance appraisals
- Lack of attention to detail in funds management

The Administrative Judge further determined that the Complainant failed to identify similarly situated employees who received more favorable treatment. The Complainant cited two coworkers who were not disciplined for a physical altercation in front of patrons; however, the Administrative Judge found these individuals were not adequately comparable, as they held different positions and the Complainant's termination was based on an entirely different set of circumstances and reasons.

### Hostile Work Environment and Harassment Claims

The Complainant alleged a hostile work environment based on the following incidents:

1. S1's undocumented verbal counselings and subsequent reference to them in the Notice of Proposed Removal
2. S1's issuance of a Letter of Reprimand regarding the Complainant leaving the library unattended for a personal matter
3. S1's acceptance of allegedly inaccurate statements from subordinates without further investigation
4. The Complainant's proposed removal and ultimate termination

#### Failure to Establish Nexus to Protected Bases

The Administrative Judge found that the Complainant failed to establish any nexus between the alleged incidents and her protected bases of race, sex, color, or age. With respect to sex and age, the Administrative Judge determined that the Complainant offered only conclusory statements without evidentiary support. Regarding race and color, the Administrative Judge found that mere speculation based on the racial composition of the workplace—without additional evidence of racial animus—was insufficient to establish a discriminatory motive.

The Administrative Judge acknowledged an affidavit from a coworker supporting the existence of racial hostility, which included allegations that unnamed staff members expressed dislike of being supervised by an African American and that both a subordinate and S1 criticized the Complainant's experience level compared to her Caucasian predecessor. However, the Administrative Judge found the affidavit "very confusing" and noted that the coworker had obtained this information secondhand or thirdhand rather than through personal observation. The Administrative Judge concluded that absent corroboration of these allegations, the uncorroborated statement alone was insufficient to establish racial animus.

#### Failure to Establish Severity and Pervasiveness

The Administrative Judge further found that the Complainant failed to establish that she was subjected to severe and pervasive harassment sufficient to alter her employment conditions and create an abusive working environment. The Administrative Judge characterized the incidents as ordinary workplace disputes, including disagreements with supervisors, supervisory management attempts, communication problems, and the implementation of progressive discipline.

An Agency Chief Human Resources Officer stated in an affidavit that verbal counseling is not required to be documented in personnel files, supporting the conclusion that S1's undocumented counselings did not constitute a violation of Agency policy or grounds for harassment findings.

## Conclusions

The Administrative Judge concluded that the Complainant failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that she was subjected to employment discrimination or a hostile work environment based on race, sex, color, or age. The Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the employment actions, and the Complainant provided insufficient evidence to establish that these reasons were pretextual or that she was treated differently based on a protected characteristic.
