items.source: During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Contract Specialist-GS-11 at the Agency’s facility in Gallup, New Mexico. On August 25, 2015, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on race (Native American), national origin (Native American), age, and in reprisal for protected activity (instant EEO complaint). By letter dated November 23, 2015, the Agency accepted the formal complaint for investigation. After an investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing. Over Complainant's objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s March 22, 2018 motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision by summary judgment on September 23, 2020. In her decision, the AJ framed the claims in the following fashion: 1. On or about May 15 and June 3, 2015, Complainant was denied FAC-C Level II training and certification. 2 2. Denial of the May 15 and June 3, 2015 training and certification impaired Complainant’s ability to qualify for advancement and promotion, including but not limited to those asserted in claims 3, 4, 7-8, 10-11, and 13-17 herein. 3. On or about June 2, 2015, Complainant was denied promotion to Job Announcement No. CV-15-PQ-1406482(MP), Contract Specialist, GS-1102-11/13. 4. On June 8, 2015, Complainant learned she was not selected for Job Announcement No. CV-15-PQ1360171(MP), Contract Specialist, GS-1102-11/13. 5. On or about September 10, 2015, Complainant was denied FAC-C Level II training and certification. 6. Denial of the September 10, 2015 training and certification impaired Complainant’s ability to qualify for advancement and promotion, including but not limited to those asserted in claims 3, 4, 7-8, 10-11, and 13-17 herein. 7. On or about October 20, 2015, Complainant was not selected for Job Announcement No. 1507681. 8. On or about November 30, 2015, Complainant was not selected for Job Announcement Number CV-16-PQ1538101(MP). 9. On or about April 4, 2016, Complainant’s FAC-C certification and warrant were not renewed. 10. On or about April 4, 2016, Complainant was not selected for Job Announcement Number CV-16-PQ11624675(MP). The FAC-C program established education, experience, and training standards for the federal government acquisition workforce. 11. On or about April 4, 2016, Complainant was not referred for Job Announcement Number CV-16-PQ1651114 (MP). 12. On or about May 2, 2016, [C1], an officer of the Agency, subjected Complainant to harassment by hugging her without permission, and in the presence of other Agency personnel. 13. On or about May 13, 2016, the Agency did not select Complainant for Job Announcement Number CV-16-PQ1671191(MP). 14. On or about May 16, 2016, the Agency did not select Complainant for a position in Albuquerque, New Mexico, Announcement Number CRPA 78/16. 15. On or about May 16, 2016, the Agency did not select Complainant for a position in Gallup, New Mexico, Announcement Number CRPA 81/16. 16. On or about June 9, 2016, the Agency did not select Complainant for two vacancies in Reston, Virginia, Job Announcement Numbers CV-16PQ1696209(MP) and CV- 16-PQ1696241 (MP). 17. On or about August 29, 2016, the Agency did not select Complainant for a Contract Specialist vacancy in Reston, Virginia Job Announcement Number PQ1719227. 18. On or about April 18, 2017, the Agency denied Complainant permission to attend training, specifically CON 290, Contract Administration and Negotiation Techniques, scheduled for April 24, 2017-May 5, 2017, at BIA Southwest Region, Albuquerque, New Mexico. 19. From April 18, 2017-May 4, 2018, the Agency delayed approval of Complainant’s leave requests, and then made approval contingent on completing certain work. 20. On or about April 18, 2017, the Agency informed Complainant that she would not be permitted to obtain a Level II FAC-C warrant without [Bureau Procurement Chief’s, (C1’s)] approval. The AJ found that Complainant failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination and/or reprisal with respect to claims 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14, and 16. Regarding claim 8, the AJ found that Complainant did not apply and submit an application for the position. Regarding claims 3, 4, 7, 11, 13, and 16, the AJ reasoned that Complainant did not meet the minimum qualifications because she did not have the Level II and Level III FAC-C certifications. Regarding claim (14), the AJ reasoned that Complainant did not establish a prima face case of discrimination and/or retaliation because the selectee was of the same national origin and sex of Complainant. In addition, the selectee for claim 14, was older than Complainant. Moreover, the AJ found that there was no evidence that the selecting official for claim 14 was aware of Complainant’s EEO activity. The AJ found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions and Complainant failed to establish pretext with respect to claims 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 19, 15, and 17-20. Finally, regarding claim 12, that C1 hugged Complainant, the AJ noted that Complainant did not claim that there were any sexual aspects of the hug. The AJ found that there is no evidence that Complainant’s protected classes motivated the hug. In addition, the AJ found that this single act was not sufficiently severe or pervasive to create a hostile work environment. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant, though her attorney, asserts that the Agency systemically denied promotions to qualified Native Americans. Complainant, in her brief, asserts that C1 decided that her 17-hour class on Analyzing Contract Costs was insufficient for Level II certification, even though another named Agency official approved it. Complainant also asserted that C1 decided, without OPM approval, that future contracting jobs would require Level II certification. ## Background and Procedural History

The Complainant, a Native American female employed as a Contract Specialist-GS-11 at the Agency's Gallup, New Mexico facility, filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint on August 25, 2015, alleging discrimination and reprisal based on race (Native American), national origin (Native American), age, and protected activity. Following investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with the investigation report and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). The Complainant timely requested a hearing. Without holding a hearing, the AJ issued a decision by summary judgment on September 23, 2020, finding no discrimination. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ's decision, prompting this appeal.

## Claims Addressed

The complaint encompassed twenty enumerated claims spanning the period from May 2015 through May 2018, including: (1) denial of FAC-C Level II training and certification on multiple occasions; (2) non-selection for various promotions and job announcements; (3) denial of permission to attend training; (4) delayed approval of leave requests; and (5) harassment allegedly based on protected class status.

## Administrative Judge's Analysis and Determinations

The AJ made the following key determinations:

**Promotion and Selection Claims (3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14, 16):** The AJ found that the Complainant failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination regarding these claims. With respect to claims 3, 4, 7, 11, 13, and 16, the AJ determined that the Complainant did not meet minimum qualifications because she lacked the required FAC-C Level II and Level III certifications. The Agency requests affirmance of the final order based on the AJ's finding of no discrimination.

# FINDINGS

## Background

The Complainant worked as a Senior Special Agent, Polygraph Examiner in the Forensic Services Division at the Agency's Washington, D.C. office. On January 2, 2020, the Complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging discrimination and retaliation for prior protected EEO activity. The Agency accepted the complaint for investigation on March 11, 2020, identifying three primary claims for investigation.

## Procedural Issues

### Timeliness of Final Decision

The Complainant contends that the Agency's final decision was issued untimely, having submitted his request for a final decision on July 10, 2020. The Complainant requests imposition of default judgment as a sanction for this alleged delay. The Agency asserts that any delay in issuing its final decision was minimal and does not warrant sanctions. Based on the record provided, the Agency did issue a final decision and provided the Complainant with notice of his right to an EEOC Administrative Judge hearing in accordance with 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b).

### Adequacy of the Report of Investigation

The Complainant challenges the adequacy of the Agency's Report of Investigation, asserting that the investigation was insufficient. The Complainant notes that one management official did not respond to a request to provide testimony. This allegation requires examination of whether the investigation was conducted thoroughly and in compliance with procedural requirements.

## Substantive Claims

### Claim 1: Merit Promotion Plan Supervisory Evaluation Discrimination

The Complainant contends that he received an unfavorable 2019 MPP Supervisory Evaluation rating compared to his prior 2018 rating. The Agency determined that legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons supported the 2019 rating decision.

The Complainant asserts that this rating constitutes a continuation of prior retaliation, noting that he received an "Outstanding" rating on his 2019-2020 annual performance appraisal approximately three months prior to his MPP SE rating. The Complainant further asserts that the MPP SE represents retaliatory action based on his prior EEO complaints.

The Agency contends that the MPP SE is a separate and distinct process from the annual performance evaluation process and notes that the same supervisor (S2) did not complete the Complainant's 2018-2019 MPP SE.

### Claim 2(a) and 2(b): Quality Control and Mentoring Duties

The Complainant alleged that on or about September 10, 2019, the Agency obstructed his return to Quality Control and mentor duties, and that on September 13, 2019, his request for reconsideration was denied.

The Agency asserts that the Complainant was approved to resume mentoring duties and has been restored to such duties. Regarding Quality Control duties, the Agency states that the Complainant remains eligible for consideration but that various factors are evaluated when selecting employees for QC assignments. The Agency further asserts that no commitment regarding QC assignment was made in the prior EEO case referenced by the Complainant, though the record indicates that a prior final decision ordered the Agency to reassign the Complainant to Quality Control.

### Claim 2(c): Exclusion from Communications and Assignment Delegation

The Complainant alleged that since September 1, 2019, supervisory personnel have delegated assignments directly to Washington Field Office examiners while excluding him from these communications, thereby circumventing his role as the designated Senior Polygraph Examiner/Polygraph Backup.

The Agency asserts that S2 denied ever consulting exclusively with the Washington Field Office examiner or excluding the Complainant from communications, and further asserts that the Complainant has not been treated differently from other examiners in this regard.

## Prior EEO Case Compliance

The Complainant asserts that a prior final EEO decision ordered the Agency to reassign him to Quality Control duties and to provide EEO training to specified management officials, but that these remedies have not been implemented. This allegation raises questions regarding the Agency's compliance with prior Administrative Judge or final agency decisions.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-0343-13 Management Analyst in the Agency’s Acquisitions Policy Oversight and Business Strategies Division, Office of the Senior Procurement Executive (OSPE), Office of the Secretary (OST) in Washington, D.C. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 210-16. Complainant filed a prior EEO complaint in 2016, and she alleged that she has been subjected to ongoing retaliation since filing her complaint. ROI at 112. Complainant alleged that, although the Agency completed a desk audit of her position in 2016 and determined that her position was properly graded at the GS-13 level, there were inaccuracies in her position description under the “Scope and Effect” and “Supervisory Controls” sections. ROI at 115, 218-28. Complainant stated that she repeatedly raised these inaccuracies with management beginning in February 2017, to no avail. ROI at 115. The OSPE Deputy Director (DD-1) stated that she met with Complainant on February 6, 2017, as Complainant was preparing to return to OSPE from a detail. ROI at 139. According to DD-1, after Complainant asked her to look at inaccuracies in her position description, she reviewed Complainant’s position description with Human Resources and determined that the position description accurately reflected the responsibilities and duties of Complainant’s position. ROI at 139. Complainant averred that neither DD-1 nor the Associate Director of the Acquisition Policy Oversight and Business Strategies Division (AD), Complainant’s new supervisor as of June 2018, knew her actual job duties because they were new to OSPE and, therefore, were not qualified to assess her position description. ROI at 127. According to Complainant, the M-60 shared drive is a shared drive for employees and contractors to archive non-personnel-related work documentation. ROI at 116. Complainant stated that in June 2017, she noticed that a coworker (Coworker) had saved her investigative affidavit for Complainant’s prior EEO complaint to the M-60 shared drive. ROI at 116. Complainant alleged that the affidavit was posted on the shared drive to harm her reputation by making it visible to everyone in the office. ROI at 116. Complainant averred that she took a screenshot of the affidavit, deleted the affidavit from the shared drive, and reported it to DD-1. DD-1 stated that Coworker inadvertently saved a copy of the affidavit to the shared drive and that she directed Coworker to delete it from the shared drive immediately after it was brought to her attention. ROI at 139-40. Coworker averred that she accidentally saved a copy of her affidavit for Complainant’s EEO complaint to the M-61 shared drive. 2 ROI at 538. According to Coworker, she meant to save it to her personal “H” drive and did not realize she had saved it to the shared “S” drive until DD-1 brought the matter to her attention. ROI at 538. Complainant alleged that DD-1 should have disciplined Coworker. ROI at 127. Complainant stated that she told AD several times that she needed to speak with her attorney before she could provide information about the Digital IT Acquisition Program. ROI at 117. According to Complainant, this was because the Digital IT Acquisition Program was related to her prior EEO complaint. ROI at 117. Complainant averred that on June 29, 2018, AD met with her to discuss the matter, and AD questioned Complainant as though it was an interrogation. ROI at 117. Complainant stated that she left AD’s office and returned to her cubicle, only to receive another email from AD within minutes. ROI at 117. Complainant alleged that, when she went to AD’s doorway to ask why she was doing this, AD responded that Complainant believed everyone was out to get her. ROI at 117. AD stated that Complainant had indicated that she was unable to complete a work assignment because her attorney had advised her not to respond. Coworker stated that she does not have access to the M-60 shared drive and that she accidentally saved the affidavit to the M-61 shared drive. ROI at 538. However, Complainant provided a screenshot that shows the affidavit on the M-60 shared drive. ROI at 64. ROI at 163, 172. According to AD, when she asked Complainant why she could not complete the assignment during the June 29, 2018, meeting, Complainant told her that she had a pending EEO complaint related to the topic of the assignment. ROI at 163. AD averred that, during the meeting, Complainant had stated that she had not enjoyed working for her previous supervisors, as she thought they had treated her unfairly. ROI at 165. # FINDINGS

## Background and Procedural History

At the time of the events giving rise to this complaint, the Complainant was employed as a GS-0343-13 Management Analyst in the Agency's Acquisitions Policy Oversight and Business Strategies Division, Office of the Senior Procurement Executive, Office of the Secretary in Washington, D.C. Complainant filed a prior EEO complaint in 2016 and subsequently filed the subject complaint on October 2, 2018, alleging reprisal for protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

## Factual Findings

### Position Description Inaccuracies (February 2017)

A desk audit completed by the Agency in 2016 determined that Complainant's position was properly graded at the GS-13 level. However, Complainant identified inaccuracies in the "Scope and Effect" and "Supervisory Controls" sections of her position description. Beginning in February 2017, Complainant repeatedly raised these inaccuracies with management.

The OSPE Deputy Director (DD-1) met with Complainant on February 6, 2017, reviewed the position description with Human Resources, and determined that the position description accurately reflected Complainant's responsibilities and duties. Complainant disputed this assessment, arguing that DD-1 and the Associate Director (AD), Complainant's supervisor as of June 2018, were not sufficiently familiar with her actual job duties to make an informed determination, as both were relatively new to OSPE.

### Affidavit Posted on Shared Drive (June 2017)

In June 2017, Complainant discovered that a coworker (Coworker) had saved Complainant's investigative affidavit from her prior EEO complaint to the M-60 shared drive. Complainant alleged the affidavit was intentionally posted to harm her reputation by making it visible to all office employees.

The investigation revealed a factual discrepancy. Coworker stated she does not have access to the M-60 shared drive and that she accidentally saved the affidavit to the M-61 shared drive, intending to save it to her personal "H" drive. However, Complainant provided a screenshot showing the affidavit on the M-60 shared drive. DD-1 stated that Coworker inadvertently saved the affidavit and that she immediately directed Coworker to delete it upon learning of the matter. Complainant alleged DD-1 should have disciplined Coworker for this incident.

### June 29, 2018 Meeting Between Complainant and AD

Complainant alleged that on June 29, 2018, AD questioned her regarding the Digital IT Acquisition Program in an interrogatory manner after Complainant repeatedly stated she needed to consult her attorney before providing information, as the program was related to her prior EEO complaint. Complainant further alleged that AD responded to her inquiry about the subsequent email by stating, "you think everyone is out to get you."

AD provided a different account, stating that Complainant had indicated she was unable to complete a work assignment because her attorney had advised her not to respond. AD stated that during the meeting, Complainant disclosed she had a pending EEO complaint related to the assignment topic and expressed that she had not enjoyed working for previous supervisors due to perceived unfair treatment. AD denied making the statement attributed to her and stated instead that she was referencing Complainant's perceived unfair treatment in the office generally.

### Micromanagement, Over-management, and Telework Restrictions (July 2018)

Complainant alleged she was subjected to excessive micromanagement and over-management, citing the example that in September 2018, DD-1 and AD requested additional documentation for approvals regarding the Warrior to DOT Contracting Intern Program (W2DOT Program) and subsequently failed to respond to Complainant's approval requests.

DD-1 stated that she repeatedly requested Complainant produce a consolidated program/project schedule for the W2DOT Program, which Complainant complained was micromanagement but never adequately provided.

Regarding telework, Complainant alleged the new telework policy was more restrictive for employees with "ad hoc" telework agreements, limiting them to one day per week with supervisory notification. DD-1 stated that Complainant maintained a "very liberal ad hoc telework schedule" and that no restrictions were placed on her telework following implementation of the OSPE Timekeeping and Telework Standard Operating Procedure on July 1, 2018. AD confirmed that Complainant's pre-existing telework schedule was "grandfathered" in under the new policy.

### FAC-P/PM-IT Certification Application Denial (July 8, 2018)

Complainant alleged that although she completed all required training for the Federal Acquisition Certification for Program and Project Managers Information Technology Core-Plus Specialization (FAC-P/PM-IT), AD denied her application without explanation.

AD and DD-1 stated that FAC-P/PM-IT certification is not required for Complainant's position. According to Agency policy, this specialized certification is intended primarily for those responsible for acquisition of IT investments. AD averred that Complainant's position does not entail such responsibility and that the application did not document the required minimum two years of relevant experience.

### Request for Supervisory Reassignment (July-August 2018)

Complainant requested reassignment to a supervisor outside the chain of command of DD-1 and AD, and subsequently requested a detail assignment to the Assistant Secretary for Administration (M) during summer 2018. Both requests were denied—the latter based on inadequate resources to fulfill Complainant's duties.

Complainant later clarified that she was not detailed to M, contrary to one of her original allegations. DD-1 stated that Complainant requested to directly report to the Senior Procurement Executive (SPE), but the SPE denied this request. DD-1 noted that Complainant proposed two alternative supervisors, but on August 7, 2018, advised her that neither was a logical option given her duties and urged her to improve her working relationship with AD, noting that AD had been her supervisor for only approximately one month. Complainant contended that DD-1 should not have been involved in reviewing her request for reassignment away from DD-1's chain of command.

### Request to Participate in Agile Panel (September 2018)

Complainant alleged that after being invited to speak on a panel regarding Agile initiatives, AD marginalized the event and prevented Complainant from participating as a speaker.

AD stated she denied Complainant's request to speak because OSPE had not undertaken substantial Agile initiatives beyond limited-scope events and offered Complainant the opportunity to participate as an audience member. DD-1 stated the panel was organized by a contractor to discuss changes for federal employees as agencies adopted Agile Unleashed, and that because OSPE had implemented no Agency-specific Agile initiatives beyond technology, Complainant lacked relevant Agency-specific knowledge to contribute.

## Procedural Issues on Appeal

Complainant challenges the adequacy of the investigative record and requests sanctions against the Agency. The Agency counters that the record is complete and notes that Complainant failed to submit requested documents to the investigator, failed to raise deficiencies upon reviewing the investigative record, and withdrew her hearing request the day before discovery was scheduled to commence. The Agency asserts that evidence Complainant provided on appeal was reasonably available during the investigation and should not be considered.

Complainant was employed by the Agency as a Legal Assistant (Court), GS-0986-08, at the Orlando Immigration Court in Orlando, Florida. on his race (African-American), sex (male), and reprisal (prior protected EEO activity under Title VII, the ADEA, and the Rehabilitation Act) when on October 22, 2015: • He got a mid-year review by his first line supervisor (“S1” – Hispanic, female, Supervisory Legal Assistant) that negatively and falsely characterized his professionalism and customer service with a list of untrue and twisted distortions; and • He was not permitted to give evidence refuting the mid-year review. On November 5, 2015, Complainant filed EEO complaint EOI-2016-00061 (“Complaint 2”) alleging he was subjected to discrimination and a hostile work environment on the above bases and age (49) when on October 22, 2015: • He got his mid-year review in a conference room rather than in S1’s office; • His second line supervisor (“S2” – Caucasian, male, Court Administrator) was present in the conference room. Following separate EEO investigations on Complaints 1 and 2, Complainant requested a hearing on each before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ), and they were later joined. The Agency filed a motion for summary judgement, which Complainant opposed. The AJ granted the motion and found no discrimination without a hearing, and the Agency adopted this decision in its final order. The instant appeal followed the AJ’s decision. In the mid-term review, S1 assessed Complainant’s performance as “at a successful level or higher.” Complainant contended he unfairly did not receive a rating of Excellent or Outstanding. The AJ found it uncontroverted that EOIR employees do not receive a rating of record at their mid-year review. In the narrative portion of Complainant’s mid-year review, S1 wrote for the critical performance element of “Customer Service” that he needed to communicate with attorneys and return telephone calls, for the critical performance element of “Establish, Update, Maintain and Process Record of Proceedings and Case Records” he needed to keep up with motions – not hold them, and not sign nor let orders sit overnight on his desk, and for the critical element of “Legal and Technical Support” he needed to be a team player by limiting his cell phone and internet usage. S1 also wrote that Complainant should continue his hard work and continue to strive for excellence. The AJ found that Complainant only contested the assessment of his Customer Service. In support his claim that the mid-year review was falsely critical, Complainant pointed to a September 2015 letter by a defendant to an immigration judge complimenting her handling of his case for nearly five years, and expressing, without a name, his “thankfulness… to your direct assistant, who was always very friendly and correct in handling my affairs.” Complainant started assisting this judge in June 2014, when he was hired by EOIR. He alleged that on October 22, 2015, S2 refused to accept this letter, explaining it “failed… as creditable” evidence. Report of Investigation (ROI) Complaint 1, Bates No. 10 (EEO complaint) and Bates Nos. 90 – 91, at ¶¶ 24 – 27 (Complainant’s affidavit). The AJ found assuming Complainant tried to submit this letter, it would not have changed his rating since none is given at the mid-year review, nor refuted he needed to better communicate with attorneys and return telephone calls since it only concerned his interaction with a defendant in court. Mid-year reviews are typically given in a first line supervisor’s office. Complainant’s mid-year review was in a lower conference room away from his peers and others, giving privacy. Complainant acknowledged the conference room gave privacy. The AJ found that management choose the conference room to assure privacy, not to harass or discriminate. Typically, mid-year reviews are given with only the evaluator (S1) and person receiving it present. The AJ found that S2 was present because he had a responsibility to closely monitor things between Complainant and S1 since Complainant’s misconduct with S1 was abusive and caustic, and his disciplinary issues. In his rebuttal investigatory affidavit, made after reviewing S1, S2, and a third management official’s affidavits, Complainant countered these affidavits had lies and inconsistent statements. The AJ found this did not rebut S1 and S2’s explanations for why S2 was present at the mid-year review. 2 On appeal, Complainant argues that S2 admitted treating him differently. He cites portions of S2’s investigatory affidavit that acknowledges reviews are normally done in the evaluator’s office with only the evaluator (S1) and person being evaluated present, and Complainant got different treatment on these things. Complainant “respectfully questions” whether there can be equal justice where Agency counsel and the AJ are white. He argues there are genuine issues of material fact entitling him to a hearing, citing, for example, S2’s admission that he was treated differently. In reply, the Agency argues its final order should be affirmed.

# FINDINGS

## Nature of Allegations

The complainant, an African-American male Legal Assistant employed by the Agency at the Orlando Immigration Court, filed two separate Equal Employment Opportunity complaints alleging discrimination and a hostile work environment based on race, sex, and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. The complaints were subsequently joined for hearing purposes.

## Factual Findings

**Mid-Year Review Evaluation (October 22, 2015)**

The complainant received a mid-year review from his first-line supervisor (S1), a Hispanic female Supervisory Legal Assistant. The review assessed the complainant's performance as "at a successful level or higher." Notably, EOIR employees do not receive a formal rating of record at their mid-year review. In the narrative portion, S1 identified areas for improvement in three critical performance elements: (1) Customer Service, noting the need to improve communication with attorneys and telephone call responsiveness; (2) Record Management, requiring better timeliness in processing motions and preventing documents from remaining on his desk overnight; and (3) Legal and Technical Support, requesting improved teamwork through reduced cell phone and internet usage. S1 also encouraged the complainant to continue his hard work and strive for excellence.

**Procedural Circumstances of the Review**

The mid-year review was conducted in a lower conference room rather than in S1's office. The complainant's second-line supervisor (S2), a Caucasian male Court Administrator, was present during the review. The complainant was not permitted to provide evidence refuting the review findings. The complainant subsequently attempted to submit a September 2015 letter from a case defendant praising his work as a judge's assistant; S2 rejected this letter as lacking credibility.

**Investigative Findings Regarding Alleged Discrimination**

The Administrative Judge found it uncontroverted that:

1. The choice of the conference room location was made to ensure privacy rather than to harass or discriminate against the complainant.

2. S2's presence at the review was necessitated by the complainant's documented pattern of abusive and caustic misconduct toward S1, coupled with his prior disciplinary issues, requiring close supervisory monitoring.

3. The Customer Service criticism was justified and not refuted by the defendant's letter, which addressed only the complainant's interaction with a defendant in court, not his communication with attorneys as identified in the review.

4. The complainant's assertions regarding allegedly false statements and inconsistencies in management affidavits did not rebut the stated explanations for the review procedures employed.

## Conclusion

The Administrative Judge granted the Agency's motion for summary judgment and found no evidence of discrimination on the bases of race, sex, age, or reprisal. The Agency adopted this determination in its final order. On appeal, the complainant challenges these findings, arguing that genuine issues of material fact exist and that he was treated differently from peers, entitling him to a hearing.
